recipes.name: Sindhi biryani
recipes.description: Sindh's bold, tangy biryani: sour-yogurt chicken layered with basmati, fried potatoes, sliced tomatoes, dried plums, mint and plenty of green chillies, then steamed on dum.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a tight lid

ingredients.name: Sindhi biryani masala or garam masala
Aloo bukhara (dried plums)
ingredients.prep: soaked in warm water for 10 minutes

ingredients.name: Saffron (or a few drops of yellow food colour)

steps.t: Rinse the basmati in several changes of cold water until the water runs almost clear, then leave it to soak in fresh water for 30 minutes. Soak the aloo bukhara in a small bowl of warm water, and crumble the saffron into the warm milk to steep.

Mix the chicken with the yogurt, ginger and garlic pastes, chilli powder, ground coriander, turmeric, half the biryani masala and the salt. Leave to marinate for at least 30 minutes, or covered in the fridge for up to 12 hours; the slightly sour yogurt gives Sindhi biryani its tang.

Heat the oil in the large heavy pot over medium-high heat. Fry the potato halves, turning them, until golden on all sides but still firm in the centre, 6–8 minutes, then lift them out with a slotted spoon. They finish cooking in the steam later.

Add the onions to the same oil and fry, stirring more often as they colour, until evenly deep golden brown, 12–15 minutes. Lift out about a third onto kitchen paper for layering. Add the cinnamon, bay leaves, cloves, both cardamoms, peppercorns and cumin seeds to the pot and stir for 30 seconds, until they crackle and smell fragrant.

Add the chopped tomatoes and cook for 4–5 minutes, mashing them, until soft. Add the chicken with all its marinade, turn the heat to high and stir-fry for 5 minutes. Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 15–20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the chicken is nearly tender and the masala is thick, with oil glistening at the edges.

Stir in the remaining biryani masala, the fried potatoes, the drained aloo bukhara and the green chillies. Cover and cook for 5 minutes more. Taste: the masala should be boldly salty and spicy, because the rice will absorb a lot of it.

Meanwhile, bring at least 3 litres of water to a rolling boil with the 2 tablespoons of salt. Add the drained rice and boil for 5–6 minutes, until the grains have lengthened and one pressed between your fingers breaks with a firm white core (about 70% cooked). Drain at once.

Spoon out half the chicken masala into a bowl. Spread a third of the rice over the masala left in the pot, then lay over the tomato slices with half the mint, coriander and reserved onions. Add the masala from the bowl, the rest of the herbs and onions, then the remaining rice. Drizzle the saffron milk (and the kewra water, if using) over the top in streaks.

Seal the pot with foil and press the lid on firmly. Cook on high heat for 2–3 minutes, until you hear a steady sizzle and see steam at the edges, then turn the heat to its lowest (set the pot on a flat griddle if your flame runs hot) and steam (dum) for 18–20 minutes, until the rice is fully tender and fluffy.

Leave the pot sealed off the heat for 5 minutes. Lift the layers out with a wide spoon from the side, so every plate gets rice, chicken, potato and plum. Check a thick piece near the bone: the meat should be white throughout with clear juices. Serve with raita and kachumber salad.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Mutton version: use 1 kg bone-in goat and simmer it in the masala, covered, for 60–70 minutes until tender before adding the potatoes and plums.
Aloo bukhara are sour-sweet dried plums sold in South Asian shops; ordinary prunes are sweeter, so add a squeeze of lemon if you use them.

recipes.name: Namak mandi karahi (Peshawari lamb karahi)
recipes.description: The karahi of Peshawar's Namak Mandi: lamb seared in its own fat with just salt, then cooked down with whole tomatoes, black pepper and green chillies. No onions and almost no spices, so the meat leads.
equipment: Karahi or wide heavy wok with a lid

ingredients.name: Lamb shoulder, leg or ribs, bone-in or boneless

steps.t: Pat the lamb dry with kitchen paper and trim off any thick silver skin, but keep the fat: in Namak Mandi the meat cooks in rendered tail fat, and that fat carries the flavour. If your lamb is lean, the ghee stands in for it.

Heat the fat or ghee in the karahi over high heat until shimmering. Add the lamb and salt and stir-fry for 8–10 minutes, turning the pieces, until browned all over. The meat releases a lot of liquid at first; keep the heat high until it has bubbled away and the lamb sizzles again.

Pour in the water, cover tightly and cook over low heat for 35–45 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes and adding a splash more water only if the pan runs dry. The lamb is ready for the next stage when a knife slides in easily but the meat still holds its shape.
Lay the tomatoes on top of the meat, cover again and cook for 6–8 minutes, until their skins split. Lift the loose skins away with tongs and discard them.

Uncover, turn the heat up to high and keep stirring and pressing the tomatoes against the sides of the karahi for 8–10 minutes (this constant frying is called bhunai). Stop when the tomatoes have melted into a thick, glossy masala that clings to the lamb and the fat separates out at the edges.
Stir in the crushed black pepper and green chillies and cook for 2–3 minutes more. Taste for salt: the dish should taste of lamb, pepper and tomato rather than spice.
Scatter over the ginger matchsticks and serve straight from the karahi with hot naan, sliced raw onion and lemon wedges.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Mutton (goat) works the same way but needs 15–20 minutes longer in the covered stage.
Peshawari cooks rarely add garlic; a few crushed cloves in step 2 are a common home addition.

recipes.name: Chapli kebab
recipes.description: Peshawar's famous flat beef kebabs, studded with crushed coriander, pomegranate seeds, tomato and chilli, and shallow-fried until deeply browned with crisp, lacy edges.
equipment: Large heavy frying pan or flat griddle

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.prep: sliced into thin rounds, to press on top

ingredients.name: Oil, ghee or beef fat for shallow-frying

steps.t: Put the chopped onion in a clean cloth and squeeze out as much juice as you can, and pat the chopped tomato dry. Wet onion and tomato are the main reason chapli kebabs fall apart in the pan.

Toast the coriander and cumin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat for 1–2 minutes, shaking it, until fragrant and a shade darker. Tip into a mortar with the anardana and crush coarsely; the pieces should still be visible in the finished kebab.

Put the mince in a bowl with the onion, chopped tomato, green chillies, ginger, coriander leaves, crushed spices, chilli flakes, black pepper, maize flour, egg and salt. Knead with your hand for 2–3 minutes, until the mixture turns sticky and holds together when squeezed. Cover and chill for 30 minutes so it firms up.

With wet hands, divide the mixture into 8 balls. Flatten each between your palms into a thin round about 12 cm across and 1 cm thick, slightly thinner in the middle because it puffs as it cooks. Press a tomato slice into the centre of each.

Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat until a pinch of the mixture sizzles hard. Fry the kebabs two or three at a time, tomato side down first, for 3–4 minutes, until a dark brown crust forms and the edges look lacy and crisp. Turn them carefully with a fish slice.

Fry the second side for 3–4 minutes, until equally dark and the centre feels firm when pressed (71 °C on a thermometer). Drain briefly on a rack and keep warm in a low oven while you fry the rest, adding a little more oil if the pan looks dry.
Serve hot with naan, a yogurt raita, sliced onion and lemon wedges.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: In Peshawar the kebabs are fried in beef tallow, which gives the lacy edge; ghee is the closest home substitute.
Shaped, uncooked kebabs freeze well between sheets of baking paper; fry from frozen over slightly lower heat.

recipes.name: Balochi sajji (oven-roasted chicken)
recipes.description: Balochistan's salt-roasted chicken, rubbed simply with salt, lemon, garlic and pepper and roasted slowly until the skin is taut and golden: a home-oven take on meat roasted on skewers beside an open fire.
equipment: Roasting tin with a wire rack

steps.t: Pat the chicken dry inside and out. With a sharp knife, cut 3–4 deep slashes into each breast, thigh and drumstick, right down to the bone, so the salt can reach inside the meat.

Mix the salt, pepper, lemon juice and garlic paste (and the papaya paste and chilli, if using) and rub it all over the chicken, into the slashes and inside the cavity. Tie the legs together with string. Leave uncovered in the fridge for at least 1 hour, or up to 12 hours; the skin dries and roasts crisper.

Take the chicken out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking and heat the oven to 180 °C. Sit the bird on the rack over the roasting tin, so the heat circulates all round it like the fire it is usually roasted beside, and pour a cup of water into the tin to stop the drippings burning.
Roast on the middle shelf for 60 minutes, basting with the melted ghee every 20 minutes. The skin will slowly tighten and turn pale gold.

Turn the oven up to 220 °C and roast for 15–20 minutes more, until the skin is deep golden and crackly in places. Check the thickest part of the thigh with a thermometer: it should read at least 74 °C, and the juices should run clear when you pierce it.

Rest the chicken on a board, loosely covered with foil, for 10 minutes so the juices settle back into the meat. Cut into quarters and serve with lemon wedges, onion rings and naan; in Quetta it often comes on a mound of plain rice moistened with the pan drippings.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Traditional sajji is whole lamb or chicken on long skewers planted around a fire pit and roasted for hours, seasoned with nothing but salt.
A lamb leg (about 2 kg) can be roasted the same way at 160 °C for about 3 hours, covered for the first 2.

recipes.name: Pindi chole (Rawalpindi chickpeas)
recipes.description: Dark, tangy chickpeas from Rawalpindi, cooked with tea for colour and coated in dry-roasted spices and anardana, then finished with a sizzling ginger and chilli tempering instead of an onion-tomato gravy.
equipment: Pressure cooker or large heavy pot

ingredients.name: Dried chickpeas (kabuli chana)
ingredients.prep: soaked overnight in plenty of water

ingredients.name: Strong black tea (2 tea bags brewed in 250 ml water)

steps.t: Drain the soaked chickpeas and put them in the pressure cooker or pot with the brewed tea, black cardamom, bay leaves, cinnamon, salt and 1 litre of water. The tea is what turns Pindi chole their characteristic deep brown.

Pressure-cook for 20–25 minutes once it reaches pressure, or simmer half-covered in the pot for 60–75 minutes, topping up with hot water as needed. They are done when a chickpea squashes easily between your thumb and finger with no chalky centre.

While the chickpeas cook, dry-roast the coriander seeds, cumin, anardana, peppercorns and cloves in the small pan over medium-low heat, shaking it, for 3–4 minutes until a shade darker and very fragrant. Cool, then grind to a fine powder with the amchur, chilli powder and garam masala.

Fish out the whole spices. Drain the chickpeas, keeping the dark cooking liquid, and return them to the pot with about 250 ml of the liquid. Stir in the ground masala, mash a ladleful of chickpeas against the side of the pot and simmer over low heat for 10 minutes, stirring, until the chickpeas are coated in a thick, almost dry masala. Add more liquid if it sticks.

For the tempering, heat the oil in the small pan over medium heat until it shimmers. Add the ginger and green chillies and fry for about 1 minute, until the ginger edges turn golden and the chillies blister. Pour the sizzling oil straight over the chickpeas.
Cover the pot for 2–3 minutes so the aroma soaks in, then stir. Pile into bowls, top with onion rings and coriander and serve with lemon wedges and hot bhature, kulcha or naan.

recipes.reheating: Reheat with a splash of water until steaming hot.
notes: Many Rawalpindi cooks finish the dish with hot ghee instead of oil; it is richer but no longer vegan.
Short of time? Use 3 cans of chickpeas, drained, simmered for 15 minutes in the tea with the whole spices.

recipes.name: Mutton yakhni pulao
recipes.description: Peshawari pulao: mutton is simmered with a pouch of whole spices into a fragrant broth (yakhni), then basmati is cooked in that broth with fried onions until every grain is perfumed and separate.
equipment: Heavy pot with a tight lid
Muslin square or large tea infuser

ingredients.name: Plain yogurt, for a Karachi-style pulao

steps.t: Tie the fennel, coriander seeds, peppercorns, black cardamom, cinnamon and bay leaves in the muslin to make a spice pouch (potli). Put the mutton, water, halved onion, garlic, ginger, pouch and salt in the large pot and bring slowly to the boil, skimming off the grey foam for the first 10 minutes so the broth stays clear.

Lower the heat, half-cover and simmer gently for 75–90 minutes, until the mutton is tender and comes away from the bone easily. Lift out the meat and strain the broth, pressing on the onion and garlic. You need 900 ml of yakhni: boil it down or top it up with water to get that amount.

Heat the oil and ghee in the heavy pot over medium-high heat. Fry the sliced onions, stirring often, until deep golden, 10–12 minutes. Add the cumin seeds, cloves and green cardamom and fry for 30 seconds, until they crackle.

Add the cooked mutton and fry it with the onions for 5 minutes, turning, until the outside is lightly browned and glossy; this frying (bhunai) deepens the flavour. For the Karachi style, stir in the yogurt now and cook for 3–4 minutes until it no longer looks wet.

Pour in the 900 ml of hot yakhni and season it boldly (it should taste slightly too salty, as the rice absorbs a lot), then bring to a rolling boil. Add the drained rice and green chillies, stir once gently and boil uncovered over high heat for 6–8 minutes, until the liquid has dropped below the surface of the rice and small steam holes appear.

Sprinkle over the garam masala, cover tightly (wrap the lid in a tea towel or seal the pot with foil) and cook over the lowest heat for 15 minutes. Turn off the heat and leave it covered for 5 minutes more.

Fluff the rice gently from the sides with a fork, bringing the mutton up from the bottom. Every grain should be separate and tender with no hard centre. Serve with raita, kachumber salad and lemon wedges.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
safety: Cook mutton (goat) until browned on the outside; slow-cooked pieces are safe once tender and steaming hot throughout.
notes: Chicken yakhni pulao follows the same method with 1 kg bone-in chicken simmered for 30 minutes for the broth.
Leftover yakhni makes a restorative winter soup with a squeeze of lemon and black pepper.

recipes.name: Chicken jalfrezi
recipes.description: A fast, hot stir-fried curry of boneless chicken with crunchy peppers, onion petals and tomato in a thick, tangy masala; a weeknight favourite in Pakistani homes.

ingredients.name: Onions
ingredients.prep: 1 finely chopped, 1 cut into 2 cm petals

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.prep: half grated, half cut into matchsticks

steps.t: Cut everything before you light the stove, because jalfrezi is cooked fast over high heat: slice the chicken into strips, cut one onion into petals and chop the other finely, slice the peppers and purée two of the tomatoes.

Heat 2 tablespoons of the oil in the karahi over high heat until it shimmers. Add the chicken in one layer and sear for 3–4 minutes, turning once, until lightly browned but not cooked through. Lift it onto a plate.

Add the rest of the oil and the cumin seeds; when they sizzle, add the chopped onion and fry over medium-high heat for 4–5 minutes until soft and golden at the edges. Add the grated ginger and the garlic paste and stir for 30 seconds, until the raw smell goes.

Add the puréed tomatoes, chilli powder, turmeric, ground coriander and salt. Cook, stirring and scraping the pan, for 4–5 minutes, until the masala is thick and the oil starts to separate at the edges. Splash in a little water if it catches.

Return the chicken and its juices and cook for 2–3 minutes. Add the peppers, onion petals, tomato wedges and green chillies and toss over high heat for 3–4 minutes, so the vegetables are hot and glossy but still crunchy and the chicken is cooked through (74 °C, no pink in the centre).
Stir in the vinegar, garam masala, ginger matchsticks and coriander, take the pan off the heat and serve at once with naan, paratha or plain rice.

recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Sai bhaji (Sindhi spinach and lentils)
recipes.description: A Sindhi home classic: spinach, dill and chana dal simmered with tomatoes and a few vegetables, mashed to a coarse, silky green purée and finished with a garlic tempering.

steps.t: Heat the 3 tablespoons of oil in the heavy pot over medium heat and fry the onion for 5–6 minutes, until soft and lightly golden. Add the ginger, chopped garlic and green chillies and stir for 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes, turmeric, chilli powder, ground coriander and salt and cook for 4–5 minutes, mashing the tomatoes, until they collapse into a thick masala.

Add the drained chana dal, potato and aubergine and stir to coat them. Pile in the spinach a few handfuls at a time, letting each batch wilt before adding the next, then add the dill, kasuri methi and water.

Bring to the boil, cover and simmer over low heat for 30–35 minutes, stirring now and then, until the chana dal is completely soft and crushes easily (or pressure-cook for about 12 minutes). There should be a little liquid left, not a soup.
Mash everything in the pot with the masher until you have a coarse, thick purée with a few soft pieces of potato and dal still visible. If it looks watery, simmer uncovered for 3–4 minutes, stirring.

For the tempering, heat the tablespoon of oil in the small pan over medium heat and fry the sliced garlic and dried chillies for about 1 minute, until the garlic is pale gold; it turns bitter if it goes brown. Pour over the sai bhaji and serve with plain rice or phulka. Sindhi families often pair it with bhugal chawal, rice cooked with browned onions.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Sai bhaji tastes even better the next day. Sorrel (khatti bhaji), bottle gourd or a few okra are traditional additions.

recipes.name: Halwa puri with chana (Lahori breakfast)
recipes.description: Lahore's Sunday breakfast: puffed fried puris with golden semolina halwa and a spiced chickpea and potato curry, eaten together in one bite.
equipment: Kadhai or deep pan for frying

ingredients.name: Plain flour (maida), or half wholewheat atta
Potato (1 medium)
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.t: Make the puri dough first. Mix the flour and salt, rub in the tablespoon of oil, then add the water a little at a time and knead for 5 minutes into a firm, smooth dough, stiffer than chapati dough so the puris puff without soaking up oil. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

For the chana, heat the oil in the saucepan over medium heat, add the cumin seeds and let them sizzle for a few seconds, then fry the onion for 7–8 minutes until golden. Add the ginger and garlic pastes, the tomatoes, chilli powder, turmeric, ground coriander and salt and cook for 5–6 minutes, mashing, until the tomatoes melt and the oil separates.

Add the chickpeas, potato and water, bring to the boil and simmer, partly covered, for 20 minutes, until the potato is tender. Mash a ladleful of chickpeas and potato against the side of the pan so the gravy turns thick and creamy, then stir in the garam masala, green chillies and coriander. Keep warm.

For the halwa, simmer the sugar, water and cardamom in a small pan for 3–4 minutes to a thin syrup, and keep it hot. Melt the ghee in the heavy saucepan over medium-low heat, add the semolina and stir constantly for 10–12 minutes, until it turns an even golden brown, smells nutty and looks loose and sandy.

Stand back and pour the hot syrup into the semolina; it will spit and steam fiercely, so use a long-handled spoon. Stir continuously for 3–4 minutes, until the syrup is absorbed and the halwa thickens, pulls away from the sides and the ghee glistens on the surface. Stir in most of the almonds, cover and keep warm.

Divide the dough into 18 balls. Roll each into a 10–12 cm round, using a smear of oil on the board instead of flour (loose flour burns in the frying oil), and keep them covered with a cloth so they don't dry out.

Heat the frying oil in the kadhai to 180 °C; a scrap of dough should rise to the surface at once. Slide in one puri and press it gently with the back of the slotted spoon until it balloons, about 20 seconds. Flip and fry for 20–30 seconds more, until golden on both sides, then drain upright in a colander. Fry the rest one at a time, letting the oil come back to temperature in between.

Serve straight away: two or three hot puris per plate with a bowl of chana and a mound of halwa topped with the remaining almonds, plus mango pickle and sliced onion if you like. Tear a piece of puri and scoop up halwa and chana in the same bite.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the halwa and chana within 2 hours and eat within 3 days; puris are best eaten within an hour.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the chana until bubbling; warm the halwa with a splash of water, stirring. Puris are best eaten fresh.
notes: Lahori halwa is often tinted orange with a few drops of food colour; leave it out for the natural golden colour.

recipes.name: Anda paratha (egg paratha)
recipes.description: A layered wholewheat paratha with spiced beaten egg cooked right onto it, crisp at the edges and soft inside: a favourite roadside breakfast with sweet milky chai.
equipment: Tawa or large heavy frying pan

steps.t: Mix the atta and salt in a bowl and add the water gradually, kneading for about 5 minutes into a soft, smooth dough that springs back when pressed. Cover and rest for 15 minutes while you prepare the eggs; resting relaxes the gluten so the paratha rolls thin without shrinking.
Beat the eggs in the wide bowl with the onion, green chilli, coriander, chilli powder and a good pinch each of salt and pepper until evenly mixed.

Divide the dough in two. Roll one piece into a 15 cm round, brush it with a teaspoon of ghee and dust lightly with flour, then fold it into thirds like a letter and fold again into a square. These folds trap layers of ghee that turn flaky. Roll the square out to about 20 cm, dusting with flour as needed.
Heat the tawa over medium-high heat. Lay the paratha on it and cook for about 1 minute, until small bubbles appear and the underside has a few brown spots. Flip and cook the second side for 1 minute.

Brush the top with ghee, then pour half the egg mix onto the paratha and spread it to the edges with a spoon. Straight away, flip the paratha so the egg side is on the tawa, drizzle a little ghee around the edges and press down with the spatula for 1½–2 minutes, until the egg is set and golden and the paratha is crisp.
Flip once more for 30 seconds, then slide onto a plate. Repeat with the second paratha. Serve hot, folded in half, with chai and ketchup or green chutney.

recipes.storage: Best eaten hot; refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: Reheat on a hot dry tawa for 1–2 minutes per side.

recipes.name: Pyaz ke pakoray (onion fritters)
recipes.description: Crisp, lacy onion fritters bound with spiced gram flour: the essential iftar snack in Pakistani homes and the rainy-day partner to a cup of chai.

steps.t: Separate the onion slices into strands in a large bowl, sprinkle with the salt and toss. Leave for 10 minutes: the salt draws out juice, which helps the batter cling without needing much water.

Add the gram flour, rice flour, green chillies, coriander, ajwain, cumin, crushed coriander, chilli flakes, turmeric and bicarbonate of soda. Toss and squeeze with your fingers until every strand is coated, then add water a spoonful at a time until you have a thick, sticky mix that just holds together, not a runny batter.

Heat the oil in the kadhai to 175 °C; a drop of batter should sizzle and rise at once. Drop in loose, rough clumps of the mixture with your fingertips, about a heaped tablespoon each, leaving spiky strands sticking out, which become the crispest bits. Fry 6–8 at a time without crowding.

Fry for 4–5 minutes, turning once or twice, until deep golden brown and crisp all over; the bubbling slows down when the moisture has cooked out. Lift out onto the rack to drain and keep the oil at temperature between batches.
Serve hot with imli (tamarind) chutney or green mint chutney and a cup of chai. Pakoray soften as they cool, so fry them just before eating.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh; refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a 200 °C oven for 5–6 minutes.

recipes.name: Gajar ka halwa (carrot halwa)
recipes.description: Winter's favourite sweet: grated red carrots slowly cooked down in milk, then fried in ghee with sugar, cardamom and nuts until glossy and deep orange-red.
equipment: Wide heavy kadhai or sauté pan

steps.t: Peel and coarsely grate the carrots. Red Delhi carrots give the classic colour and sweetness; ordinary orange carrots work too and may need a little less sugar.
Put the carrots and milk in the wide pan over medium-high heat and bring to the boil, stirring. Turn the heat down to keep a lively simmer.

Cook for 45–55 minutes, stirring every few minutes and scraping the milk solids from the base and sides back into the carrots, until the milk has completely evaporated and the carrots look soft and slightly translucent. Stir more often towards the end, when it starts to catch.
Add the sugar. It melts and makes the mixture wet again; keep cooking and stirring for 10–12 minutes, until it dries out once more.

Add the ghee and fry over medium heat, stirring continuously, for 8–10 minutes, until the halwa looks glossy, deepens in colour and pulls away from the sides of the pan in one mass. Stir in the crushed cardamom.
Stir in the raisins and most of the almonds and pistachios. Serve warm, scattered with the remaining nuts, on its own or with a spoonful of cream.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate in a covered container within 2 hours; keeps 5 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently in a pan or microwave, stirring, until hot.
notes: For a richer halwa, crumble in 100 g of khoya (dried milk solids) with the ghee.

recipes.name: Kashmiri chai (pink tea)
recipes.description: Rosy-pink Kashmiri tea: green tea leaves boiled with baking soda and spices into a deep red brew, aerated, then simmered with milk and topped with crushed pistachios and almonds.

ingredients.name: Kashmiri green tea leaves (or gunpowder green tea)

steps.t: Put the tea leaves, 750 ml water, bicarbonate of soda, star anise, cardamom and cinnamon in the saucepan and bring to the boil. Boil steadily over medium heat for 15–20 minutes, until reduced by about half and a deep red-brown colour.

Now aerate it: scoop up ladlefuls of tea and pour them back into the pan from a height of 30 cm, again and again, for 2–3 minutes. Pour in the ice-cold water all at once (the shock deepens the colour), bring back to the boil and aerate again for 2–3 minutes until the brew is dark maroon.
Strain the concentrate (kehwa) and return it to the pan. You can make it ahead to this point and keep it in the fridge for 3 days.

Add the milk and salt and bring to the boil, then simmer for 5 minutes, still ladling and pouring from a height now and then. The tea turns from mauve to a soft pink as it aerates. Stir in sugar to taste.
Pour into cups and top each with crushed pistachios and almonds, and a spoonful of cream if you like. Serve hot with bakarkhani or plain biscuits.

recipes.storage: The tea concentrate keeps 3 days in the fridge; make the milky tea fresh.
notes: In Kashmir itself, noon chai is drunk salty rather than sweet; in Pakistani cities the sweet version is served at weddings and on winter evenings.

recipes.name: Kachumber salad
recipes.description: A crunchy chopped salad of cucumber, tomato and onion with green chilli, herbs, lemon and roasted cumin: the fresh side to every biryani, pulao and karahi.

ingredients.name: Cucumber
ingredients.prep: deseeded and cut into 1 cm dice

ingredients.name: Tomatoes
ingredients.prep: deseeded and cut into 1 cm dice

steps.t: Dice the cucumber and tomatoes into even 1 cm pieces, scooping out the watery seeds first so the salad stays crisp instead of swimming in juice. Chop the onion finely; soak it in iced water for 10 minutes and drain if you want it milder.
Toast the cumin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat for about 1 minute until fragrant and a shade darker, then crush them. Roasted cumin is what gives kachumber its smoky, savoury note.
Put the cucumber, tomatoes, onion, green chilli, coriander and mint in the bowl. Sprinkle over the roasted cumin and chilli powder.

Add the lemon juice, salt and pepper only when you are ready to eat, because salt draws the water out of the vegetables. Toss well, taste, and serve within 15 minutes alongside biryani, pulao, karahi or kebabs.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh; undressed chopped vegetables keep 1 day in the fridge.

recipes.name: Chapshuro (Hunza meat-filled bread)
recipes.description: The meat pie of the Hunza valley: thin wholewheat dough sealed around a juicy, peppery mince filling with onion, tomato and green chilli, cooked on a griddle until crisp and cut into wedges.
equipment: Large heavy frying pan or tawa with a lid

steps.t: Mix the atta and salt, add the oil, then work in the water gradually and knead for 7–8 minutes into a smooth, soft but not sticky dough. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.

Meanwhile, mix the mince with the onion, tomato, green chillies, coriander, salt, pepper and chilli flakes, squeezing it through your fingers until evenly combined. Keep it raw; it cooks inside the bread.

Divide the dough into 4 equal pieces. Roll two of them into thin rounds about 25 cm across. Spread half the filling evenly over one round in a thin layer, leaving a 1.5 cm border, and brush the border with water.

Lay the second round on top and press out any air. Seal the edges by pressing them together, then fold and pinch the rim all the way round into a rope-like crimp so no juice escapes. Prick the top a few times with a fork. Make the second chapshuro the same way.

Heat the heavy pan over medium-low heat. Cook one chapshuro, covered, for 8–10 minutes, until the underside is golden brown with darker spots and the top looks dry. Flip it carefully with a large spatula or by sliding it onto a plate and inverting it back into the pan.

Cook the second side, covered, for another 8–10 minutes. The filling is thin, so it cooks through in this time: the bread should feel puffed and firm, and juices from a fork hole should run clear, not pink (71 °C). Repeat with the second chapshuro, keeping the first warm.
Brush the hot chapshuro generously with melted ghee or apricot oil, cut it into 6–8 wedges like a pizza and serve hot with yogurt, green chutney or a cup of salted green tea.

recipes.reheating: Reheat wedges in a dry pan over medium heat, covered, for 4–5 minutes until steaming hot.
notes: Chapshuro can also be baked: cook it on a tray at 200 °C for 20–25 minutes until golden.

recipes.name: Chicken corn soup (Pakistani-Chinese)
recipes.description: The winter street soup of Karachi and Lahore: thick, silky chicken broth with sweetcorn, shredded chicken and egg ribbons, served with chilli vinegar, soy sauce and hot sauce on the side.

ingredients.name: Sweetcorn kernels, fresh, frozen or canned (drained)
White vinegar with 2 sliced green chillies

steps.t: Put the chicken breast in the saucepan with the stock and bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat. Poach for 12–15 minutes, until cooked through (74 °C in the thickest part, no pink when cut). Lift it out, leave to cool for a few minutes, then shred finely with two forks.
Blend half the sweetcorn with a ladleful of the hot stock until creamy, then return it to the pan with the whole kernels, sugar, white pepper and salt to taste. Bring back to the boil.

Stir the cornflour mixture again (it settles), then pour it into the boiling soup in a thin stream, stirring all the time. Simmer for 1–2 minutes until the soup thickens, turns glossy and coats the back of a spoon.

Turn the heat down so the soup barely bubbles. Stir it slowly in one direction and pour in the beaten eggs in a very thin stream; they set into long, silky ribbons. Leave it alone for 30 seconds before stirring again.
Add the shredded chicken and heat through for 1 minute. Taste for salt and pepper.
Ladle into bowls and serve piping hot, letting everyone add chilli vinegar, soy sauce and chilli sauce at the table, the way street vendors do.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: A can of creamed corn (about 400 g) can replace the blended half of the sweetcorn.

recipes.name: Sheer khurma
recipes.description: The Eid morning dessert: fine vermicelli toasted in ghee and simmered in reduced milk with dates, cardamom, pistachios and almonds, served warm or chilled.

steps.t: If using hard dried dates (chuhara), soak them in warm water for 1 hour first, then pit and slice them thinly; soft dates just need pitting and slicing.

Bring the milk to the boil in the heavy saucepan with the cardamom, then simmer over medium-low heat for about 20 minutes, stirring often and scraping the bottom, until it has reduced by about a quarter and looks creamy.

Meanwhile, heat the ghee in the small pan over medium heat. Fry the almonds and pistachios for 1–2 minutes until lightly golden, add the dates and raisins for 30 seconds, until the raisins puff, then lift everything out. Add the vermicelli to the same ghee and fry, stirring, for 2–3 minutes until evenly golden brown.
Add the toasted vermicelli to the simmering milk and cook for 5–6 minutes, stirring, until the strands are soft. Stir in the sugar (and saffron, if using) until dissolved.

Add most of the fried nuts, dates and raisins and simmer for 2 minutes more. The sheer khurma should be pourable; it thickens a lot as it cools, so thin it with a splash of warm milk later if needed. Stir in the rose or kewra water off the heat.
Serve warm in small bowls on Eid morning, topped with the rest of the nuts and dates, or chill it for a few hours and serve cold.

recipes.reheating: Warm gently with a splash of milk, stirring.

recipes.name: Idli (steamed rice cakes)
recipes.description: Soft, spongy steamed cakes of fermented rice and urad dal batter: the everyday South Indian breakfast, served with sambar and coconut chutney.
equipment: Idli steamer with moulds (or a large pot with a steaming rack)

ingredients.name: Idli rice or parboiled short-grain rice

steps.t: Soak the rice in plenty of water in one bowl, and the urad dal with the fenugreek seeds in another, for 4–6 hours. Plan ahead: the batter also needs 8–14 hours to ferment, so most cooks soak in the morning, grind in the evening and steam the next morning.

Drain the urad dal and grind it with about 150 ml of ice-cold water, adding it a little at a time, for 10–15 minutes in a wet grinder (or in short bursts in a blender so it doesn't heat up), until the batter is very smooth, light and fluffy and has roughly doubled. A drop should float in a glass of water. Scrape it into the large bowl.

Drain the rice and grind it with about 250 ml of water to a batter that feels slightly gritty between your fingers, like fine semolina. Add it to the urad batter with the salt and mix well with your hand for a minute; the warmth of your hand helps fermentation start.

Cover loosely and leave in a warm place (about 30 °C, such as an oven with only the light on) for 8–14 hours, until the batter has risen by half to double, looks bubbly and smells pleasantly sour. Stir it gently once without beating out the air; it should be thick but pourable, like cake batter.

Bring 5 cm of water to the boil in the steamer. Grease the moulds lightly and fill each three-quarters full. Stack them in the steamer, cover and steam over medium-high heat for 10–12 minutes, until the tops look matte and a knife pushed into the centre comes out clean.
Turn off the heat and leave the moulds for 2 minutes, then run a wet spoon round each idli and lift it out. Serve hot, 3–4 per person, with sambar and coconut chutney.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the batter for up to 3 days and steamed idlis for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Re-steam idlis for 3–4 minutes until soft and hot.
notes: In cold kitchens fermentation can take a full day; a pinch of fenugreek and using non-iodised salt both help.

recipes.name: Masala dosa
recipes.description: Large, crisp fermented rice and lentil crêpes folded around a turmeric-yellow potato and onion filling, the pride of Udupi's vegetarian restaurants, with sambar and coconut chutney.
equipment: Cast-iron tawa or large heavy flat pan

steps.t: Soak the rice in one bowl and the urad dal, chana dal and fenugreek in another for 5 hours. Drain the dal and grind it with cold water, a little at a time, until very smooth and fluffy, then grind the rice until almost smooth. Mix both with the salt, cover and ferment in a warm place for 8–12 hours, until bubbly, risen and pleasantly sour.
For the masala, boil the potatoes in their skins for 15–20 minutes until a knife slides in easily. Peel them while warm and crumble into rough chunks with your fingers; some lumps should remain.

Heat the oil in a saucepan over medium heat and add the mustard seeds. When they start to pop, add the urad dal, chana dal, curry leaves and asafoetida and stir until the dals turn golden, about 30 seconds. This sizzling of whole spices in hot oil is called tempering; it seasons the oil for the whole dish.

Add the onions, green chillies and ginger and cook for 5–6 minutes, until the onions are soft and translucent but not browned. Stir in the turmeric, then the potatoes, water and salt. Cook for 3–4 minutes, stirring and lightly mashing, until the masala is soft and holds together. Add the lemon juice and coriander and keep warm.

Stir the batter gently; it should flow like thick pouring cream, so add a splash of water if needed. Heat the tawa over medium-high heat until a sprinkle of water sizzles and evaporates in a second or two. Wipe the surface with a halved onion or a cloth dipped in oil, then lower the heat slightly.

Pour a ladleful of batter (about 100 ml) into the centre and immediately spread it outwards in a continuous spiral with the base of the ladle, pressing lightly, to make a thin round about 25 cm across. Drizzle a teaspoon of oil over the dosa and around the edge.

Cook without turning for 2–3 minutes, until the underside is evenly golden and crisp and the edges lift away from the pan. Spoon an eighth of the potato masala onto one half, fold the dosa over and slide it onto a plate.

Before the next dosa, sprinkle the pan with a little water and wipe it, so the batter spreads instead of clinging. Serve each dosa the moment it is made, with sambar and coconut chutney. The batter makes about 8 dosas, two per person.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate leftover batter for up to 3 days and the potato masala for 3 days; cook dosas fresh.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the potato masala until steaming hot before filling the dosas.
notes: Udupi restaurants often spread a thin layer of red chutney (dried chilli, garlic and onion) inside before adding the masala.

recipes.name: Coconut chutney
recipes.description: Fresh white coconut ground with roasted gram, green chilli and ginger, finished with a crackling tempering of mustard seeds and curry leaves: the partner to idli and dosa.

ingredients.name: Roasted gram (pottukadalai) or roasted chana dal

steps.t: If the coconut is frozen, let it thaw. Put the coconut, roasted gram, green chillies, ginger and salt in the blender with half the water.
Blend to a thick, fairly smooth paste, adding the rest of the water a little at a time. It should be spoonable, just thick enough to sit on an idli without running off. Scrape into a bowl.

For the tempering, heat the coconut oil in the small pan over medium heat. Add the mustard seeds and, when they start to pop, the urad dal, dried chilli and curry leaves. Stir for 20–30 seconds until the dal is golden and the leaves crisp (stand back, they spit).
Pour the sizzling tempering over the chutney and stir it in just before serving. Serve with idli, dosa, upma or vada.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate in a covered container and eat within 1 day; fresh coconut sours quickly.

recipes.name: Sambar (lentil and vegetable stew)
recipes.description: Tamil Nadu's tangy lentil and vegetable stew, soured with tamarind and flavoured with freshly roasted sambar powder and a mustard-seed tempering. Eat it with rice, idli or dosa.

steps.t: Cook the toor dal with the turmeric and water until completely soft: about 15 minutes in a pressure cooker once it reaches pressure, or 40–45 minutes simmering in a covered saucepan. Whisk it to a smooth, creamy purée.

While the dal cooks, make the sambar powder. Dry-roast the coriander seeds, chana dal, dried chillies, cumin, peppercorns and fenugreek in the small pan over medium-low heat for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until the dal turns golden and the spices smell toasty. Add the coconut for the last 30 seconds. Cool and grind to a fine powder.

Squeeze the soaked tamarind with your fingers to release the pulp, then strain the liquid into the large saucepan, discarding the seeds and fibres. Add the shallots, tomatoes, aubergine, pumpkin, green chilli and salt, plus 250 ml water, and simmer for 10–12 minutes, until the raw smell of tamarind has gone and the vegetables are almost tender.
Meanwhile, fry the okra in 1 teaspoon of the oil in the small pan over medium heat for 4–5 minutes, until bright green and no longer slimy, then add it to the pot.

Stir the ground sambar powder into the vegetables and cook for 2 minutes. Add the mashed dal and jaggery and simmer gently for 5 minutes, stirring now and then. The sambar should pour like a thick soup; loosen with hot water if needed. Taste for salt and sourness.

For the tempering, heat the remaining oil in the small pan over medium heat. Add the mustard seeds; when they pop, add the dried chillies, asafoetida and curry leaves and let them crackle for a few seconds. Pour over the sambar, cover for a minute, then stir in the coriander. Serve hot with rice and ghee, or with idli and dosa.

recipes.reheating: Loosen with a splash of water and reheat until bubbling.
notes: Drumsticks (moringa pods), radish, carrot and shallots are all classic sambar vegetables; use whatever mix you have, about 550 g in total.
Ready-made sambar powder (2 tablespoons) can replace the home-roasted powder.

recipes.name: Tomato rasam
recipes.description: A thin, peppery Tamil soup of tomato, tamarind and a little toor dal, sharp with garlic, cumin and black pepper; sipped from a cup or poured over rice.

steps.t: Simmer the toor dal in 250 ml of the water in the saucepan for about 15 minutes, until very soft, then mash it into the liquid. (If you are cooking sambar or dal anyway, a ladleful of its watery top works too.)
Meanwhile, pound the peppercorns, cumin and coriander seeds in the mortar to a coarse powder, then add the garlic and pound to a rough paste. Freshly crushed spices are the whole point of rasam.

Squeeze the soaked tamarind and strain its liquid into the pan with the dal. Add the tomatoes, crushed spice paste, turmeric, jaggery, salt and the remaining 500 ml of water. Bring to the boil, then simmer for 6–8 minutes, crushing the tomatoes with a spoon, until they are soft and the raw tamarind smell has gone.
Turn the heat down so the rasam just froths at the surface without boiling hard; boiling it at this stage makes it bitter. Take it off the heat as soon as a foamy layer rises.

For the tempering, heat the oil in the small pan over medium heat. Add the mustard seeds and, when they pop, the dried chillies, asafoetida and curry leaves. Pour the sizzling tempering into the rasam and add the coriander.
Cover and leave for 5 minutes so the flavours infuse. Serve hot in cups as a soup or ladle it over plain rice; it is also the classic remedy for a cold.

recipes.reheating: Reheat gently until just steaming; don't boil.

recipes.name: Kanda poha (flattened rice with onions)
recipes.description: Maharashtra's favourite quick breakfast: softened flattened rice tossed with onions, peanuts, curry leaves, turmeric and green chilli, finished with lemon and coriander.
equipment: Large frying pan or kadhai with a lid

steps.t: Put the poha in the sieve and rinse it under running water for 20–30 seconds, tossing it with your fingers, until the flakes soften but are not mushy. Leave to drain for 10 minutes; a flake should squash easily between your fingers. Sprinkle over the salt, sugar and turmeric and toss gently.
Heat the oil in the pan over medium heat and fry the peanuts for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until golden and crunchy. Lift them out with a slotted spoon, leaving the oil behind.

Add the mustard seeds to the oil and, when they pop, the cumin, curry leaves and green chillies. Stir for a few seconds, then add the onion and cook for 3–4 minutes, until soft and translucent but not browned.

Add the poha and toss gently with a spatula until it is evenly yellow; stir lightly or the flakes break into a paste. Cover and cook on low heat for 2–3 minutes so the poha steams and turns soft and fluffy.
Turn off the heat, add the lemon juice, most of the coriander and the peanuts and toss once more. Taste: it should be gently sweet, salty and tangy all at once.
Serve straight away, scattered with the remaining coriander and the grated coconut if using, with a cup of masala chai. In Maharashtra it is often topped with crunchy sev.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh; refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: Sprinkle with water and microwave, covered, until steaming hot.
notes: Kanda batata poha adds one small potato, diced and fried with the onion until tender.

recipes.name: Hyderabadi chicken dum biryani
recipes.description: Hyderabad's kacchi biryani: raw chicken marinated with yogurt, fried onions, mint and spices is sealed under part-cooked saffron basmati and the two cook together slowly in their own steam.
equipment: Heavy, wide pot with a tight lid (at least 5 litres)

ingredients.name: Shahi jeera (black cumin) or cumin seeds
Plain flour and water dough, to seal the lid (or use foil)

steps.t: Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat and fry the onions, stirring more often as they colour, for 15–18 minutes until evenly deep golden brown and crisp. Lift them onto kitchen paper with a slotted spoon; they crisp further as they cool. Keep the onion-flavoured oil.

In the heavy pot, mix the chicken with every marinade ingredient, three-quarters of the fried onions crushed between your fingers and 3 tablespoons of the onion oil. Spread it in an even layer over the base, cover and marinate for at least 2 hours in the fridge, or overnight. Take it out 30 minutes before cooking.

Soak the rice for 30 minutes. Bring 3.5 litres of water to a rolling boil with the salt, bay leaves, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon and shahi jeera, and, if sealing with dough, knead the flour with a little water into a stiff dough.

Add the drained rice to the boiling water and cook for 5–6 minutes, until the grains are about 75% done: they should break between your fingers with a hard white core. Drain well, but leave the whole spices in the rice.

Spread the hot rice over the raw chicken in an even layer without pressing it down. Scatter over the remaining fried onions and the mint, then drizzle over the melted ghee, saffron milk and kewra water.

Press the dough in a rope around the rim of the pot and push the lid down onto it to seal, or seal with two layers of foil under the lid. Cook over medium-high heat for 8–10 minutes, until you can hear the base sizzling and steam starts escaping, then turn the heat to the lowest setting and cook for 30 minutes more. A flat griddle under the pot stops the bottom burning.

Turn off the heat and leave it sealed for 10 minutes. Break the seal and check a piece of chicken from the bottom: it should be cooked through, with clear juices, and read at least 74 °C near the bone. If not, reseal and give it 10 more minutes on low.
Serve by digging a large spoon straight down to the bottom, so each portion has saffron rice, white rice and chicken with its masala. Serve with mirchi ka salan, raita or a simple onion salad.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: The dough seal is discarded; it only keeps the steam in.
Timing matters in kacchi biryani: if the rice goes in too soft, it turns mushy before the chicken cooks through.

recipes.name: Kolkata mutton biryani
recipes.description: Kolkata's gently spiced, fragrant biryani descended from the Awadhi kitchen: tender mutton, golden potatoes and boiled eggs layered with saffron basmati, kewra, nutmeg and mace.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a tight lid

steps.t: Mix the mutton with the yogurt, ginger and garlic pastes, chilli powder, half the salt and the sugar. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 2 hours, or overnight.

Rub the potato halves with the turmeric and a pinch of salt. Heat the oil in the heavy pot over medium heat and fry the potatoes for 6–8 minutes, turning, until golden all over; lift out. Roll the boiled eggs in the same oil for 1–2 minutes until lightly golden and blistered, and lift out.

Fry the onions in the same oil, stirring often, for 12–15 minutes until deep golden brown. Remove a third for layering. Add the cardamom, cloves and cinnamon to the pot and let them sizzle for 30 seconds.

Add the mutton and its marinade and cook over medium-high heat, stirring, for 10 minutes, until the yogurt has been absorbed and the meat is browned and glossy. Add the hot water and remaining salt, cover and simmer over low heat for 60–75 minutes, stirring now and then, until the mutton is tender.

Add the potatoes and garam masala, cover and cook for 15 minutes more, until a knife slides into the potatoes; the gravy should be thick and coat the meat. Tuck in the eggs and take the pot off the heat. Spoon out about half the meat, potatoes and eggs into a bowl.
Meanwhile, boil the soaked rice in 3 litres of salted water with the bay leaves for 5–6 minutes, until about 70% cooked, and drain.

Spread half the rice over the mutton left in the pot. Add the reserved meat, potatoes and eggs, then the rest of the rice. Mix the nutmeg and mace and sprinkle over, then drizzle with the ghee, saffron milk, kewra and rose water and scatter over the reserved onions.

Seal the pot with foil and the lid. Cook on medium heat for 3 minutes until it steams, then on the lowest heat for 25 minutes. Rest, sealed, for 10 minutes, then serve so everyone gets mutton, a potato half and an egg, with raita or a light salad.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
safety: Cook mutton (goat) until browned on the outside; slow-cooked pieces are safe once tender and steaming hot throughout.
notes: The potato is the hallmark of Kolkata biryani and many people's favourite part; some families also add a few drops of meetha attar (sweet perfume) with the kewra.
Chicken works too: use 1 kg bone-in pieces and cut the covered simmer in step 4 to 25 minutes.

recipes.name: Kerala fish curry (meen curry)
recipes.description: Central Kerala's fiery red fish curry: mackerel or kingfish simmered in coconut oil with shallots, ginger, curry leaves, Kashmiri chilli and smoky-sour kudampuli. Better still the next day.
equipment: Clay pot (manchatti) or heavy, wide saucepan with a lid

ingredients.name: Mackerel (ayala) or kingfish steaks
ingredients.prep: cleaned and cut into 5 cm pieces

ingredients.name: Kudampuli (Malabar tamarind), 3 pieces, or tamarind pulp

steps.t: Rinse the fish pieces and pat them dry. Soak the kudampuli (or tamarind) in the warm water for 15 minutes; kudampuli softens and gives the curry its smoky sourness.

Heat 2 tablespoons of the coconut oil in the clay pot or saucepan over medium heat. Add the mustard seeds and, when they pop, the fenugreek seeds; stir for a few seconds until they turn reddish-brown, not black, or they turn bitter.
Add the shallots, ginger, garlic, green chillies and half the curry leaves and fry for 5–6 minutes, stirring, until the shallots are soft and golden at the edges.

Turn the heat to low. Mix the chilli powder, turmeric and ground coriander with 3 tablespoons of water to a paste, add it to the pot and stir for 1–2 minutes, until the oil turns bright red and the raw spice smell has gone. Mixing the powder with water first stops it burning.
Add the kudampuli with its soaking water, the remaining water and the salt. Bring to the boil and simmer for 3–4 minutes so the gravy comes together.

Slide the fish pieces into the gravy in a single layer. Don't stir from now on, or the fish breaks; instead, hold the pot with a cloth and swirl it gently. Cover and simmer over low heat for 10–12 minutes, until the fish is opaque and flakes at the thickest part and the gravy has thickened.

Drizzle over the remaining tablespoon of coconut oil, scatter in the rest of the curry leaves, cover and take off the heat. Leave for at least 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge, before serving; the flavour deepens a lot. Serve with plain rice or boiled tapioca (kappa).

recipes.reheating: Reheat gently in the pot until bubbling, swirling rather than stirring.
notes: Kudampuli is sold in Indian shops as 'fish tamarind' or 'Malabar tamarind'; 1 tablespoon of tamarind pulp is the nearest substitute.

recipes.name: Goan fish curry
recipes.description: Goa's everyday xitt kodi: firm white fish simmered in a bright orange coconut gravy ground with Kashmiri chillies, coriander, cumin and garlic, soured with tamarind.

ingredients.name: Firm fish steaks (kingfish, pomfret or snapper)

steps.t: Rub the fish pieces with the turmeric and salt and set aside for 15 minutes while you make the paste. Soak the dried chillies in the warm water at the same time to soften them.

Put the coconut, soaked chillies with their water, coriander seeds, cumin, peppercorns, turmeric, garlic and ginger in the blender and blend for 2–3 minutes to a very smooth, bright orange paste. Stop and scrape down the sides; any graininess will show in the gravy.
Heat the coconut oil in the wide saucepan over medium heat and fry the onion for 5–6 minutes until soft and lightly golden. Add the tomato and cook for 2–3 minutes until it softens.

Add the curry paste and cook, stirring often, for 5 minutes, until it thickens, darkens slightly and the oil begins to separate at the edges. Rinse the blender with the 200 ml of water and add it to the pan.
Stir in the tamarind, green chillies and salt and simmer for 5 minutes. The gravy should be the consistency of single cream; add a splash of water if it is too thick.

Lower in the fish pieces in a single layer, spoon the gravy over them and simmer gently, covered, for 6–8 minutes, until the fish is opaque and just flakes. Shake the pan instead of stirring so the pieces stay whole.
Take off the heat and rest for 10 minutes. Serve with Goan red rice or plain white rice, and a piece of rava-fried fish on the side if you like.

recipes.reheating: Reheat gently until just bubbling.
notes: Prawns are just as traditional: add 500 g peeled prawns in step 6 and simmer for 4–5 minutes.

recipes.name: Machher jhol (Bengali fish curry)
recipes.description: The light, soupy fish curry of Bengali homes: turmeric-rubbed fish steaks fried in mustard oil, then simmered with potatoes in a thin cumin and ginger gravy scented with nigella.
equipment: Wide frying pan or kadhai with a lid

steps.t: Rub the fish with half the turmeric and half the salt and leave for 10 minutes. Rub the potato and aubergine wedges with a pinch each of turmeric and salt.

Heat the mustard oil in the pan over high heat until it just begins to smoke, then lower the heat to medium. Heating it this far mellows its sharp, raw pungency. Fry the fish in batches for 2–3 minutes per side, until golden and lightly crusted, and lift out onto a plate.
In the same oil, fry the potato wedges for 4–5 minutes and the aubergine for 2–3 minutes, until golden at the edges, and lift out.

Add the nigella seeds and green chillies to the oil and let them sizzle for a few seconds. Mix the ginger paste, cumin, coriander, chilli powder and remaining turmeric with 3 tablespoons of water, add to the pan and fry for 2 minutes, stirring, until the oil separates (Bengali cooks call this kasha). Add the tomato and cook for 2–3 minutes until soft.
Add the hot water, potatoes, remaining salt and the sugar and bring to the boil. Cover and simmer for 10 minutes, until the potatoes are almost tender.

Add the aubergine and the fried fish, spooning the gravy over the top, and simmer uncovered for 5 minutes, until the potatoes are completely tender and the fish has absorbed some of the gravy. The jhol should stay thin and soupy.
Scatter over the coriander and serve hot with plenty of plain rice, which soaks up the gravy.

recipes.reheating: Reheat gently until bubbling.
notes: Watch for bones: rohu and catla have fine bones, which Bengali diners pick out as they eat.

recipes.name: Kerala chicken stew (ishtu)
recipes.description: A mild, creamy white stew from Kerala's Syrian Christian kitchens: chicken, potatoes and carrots cooked in coconut milk with whole spices, ginger, green chillies and curry leaves. Classic with appam.
equipment: Heavy saucepan or Dutch oven with a lid

ingredients.name: Potatoes (2 medium)
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 3 cm cubes

steps.t: Shake the can of coconut milk well, then pour half into a jug and mix it with the 300 ml of water: this is the thin coconut milk for simmering. Keep the other half, undiluted, for finishing; it splits if it boils for long.
Heat 1½ tablespoons of the coconut oil in the saucepan over medium heat. Add the cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, crushed peppercorns and bay leaf and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Add the onions, ginger, garlic, green chillies and half the curry leaves and cook gently for 6–8 minutes, stirring, until the onions are soft and translucent. Keep the heat moderate: the stew should stay pale, so the onions must not brown.
Add the chicken and turn it in the onions for 3–4 minutes, until the outside of each piece has turned white.

Add the potatoes, carrot, thin coconut milk and salt. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook over low heat for 20–25 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the potatoes are tender and the chicken is cooked through (74 °C near the bone, juices clear).

Stir in the thick coconut milk and heat gently for 2–3 minutes, just until it steams; don't let it boil. Taste for salt; the stew should taste of coconut, pepper and ginger with a gentle heat from the chillies.
Take off the heat, drizzle over the remaining coconut oil and scatter over the rest of the curry leaves. Cover for 5 minutes, then serve with palappam, idiyappam (string hoppers) or bread.

recipes.reheating: Reheat gently without boiling, stirring, until steaming hot.
notes: Kerala's Christmas and Easter breakfast is appam with this stew; lamb or a vegetable-only version are just as traditional.

recipes.name: Palappam (lacy rice pancakes)
recipes.description: Kerala's bowl-shaped pancakes of fermented rice and coconut batter, crisp and lacy at the edges and soft and spongy in the centre; the classic partner to chicken stew.
equipment: Appachatti (small appam pan) or small non-stick wok with a lid

ingredients.name: Raw white rice (sona masoori or ponni)

steps.t: Drain the soaked rice. Dissolve the yeast and 1 teaspoon of the sugar in 3 tablespoons of lukewarm water and leave for 10 minutes until foamy.

Blend the soaked rice, coconut and cooked rice with the water, adding it gradually, for 3–4 minutes until the batter is completely smooth when rubbed between your fingers. The cooked rice is what makes the centres soft and spongy.

Pour the batter into the large bowl and stir in the yeast mixture and the remaining sugar. Cover and leave in a warm place for 8–10 hours, until it has doubled and is full of bubbles. Stir in the salt; the batter should be like thin pancake batter, so add a little water if it is thick.

Heat the appachatti over medium heat and wipe it with a little coconut oil. Pour in a small ladleful (about 60 ml) of batter, then immediately lift the pan by both handles and swirl it once in a circle, so a thin layer coats the sides while the rest pools thickly in the centre.

Put the pan back on the heat, cover and cook for about 2 minutes, without turning, until the edges are lacy, crisp and golden brown and the centre is set, spongy and no longer wet. Loosen with a thin spatula and lift out.
Repeat with the rest of the batter, greasing the pan only every few appams. Serve straight away, while the edges are crisp, with Kerala chicken stew, egg roast or sweetened coconut milk.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the batter for up to 2 days; appams are best eaten fresh.
recipes.reheating: Warm appams for a few seconds in a covered pan; the edges soften.
notes: Traditionally the batter is leavened with toddy (palm wine); yeast gives the same lift without alcohol.

recipes.name: Chicken xacuti
recipes.description: Goa's richest chicken curry: a dark, complex masala of roasted coconut, poppy seeds, Kashmiri chillies and a dozen whole spices, simmered with chicken until thick and glossy.

steps.t: Rub the chicken with the turmeric, lemon juice and salt and leave for 30 minutes while you make the masala.

Dry-roast the chillies, coriander seeds, cumin, fennel, peppercorns, cloves, cinnamon and star anise in the frying pan over medium-low heat for 3–4 minutes, shaking the pan, until fragrant and a shade darker. Add the poppy seeds for the last minute. Tip onto a plate.

Heat the tablespoon of oil in the same pan over medium heat. Add the coconut and sliced onion and roast, stirring constantly, for 10–12 minutes, until both are an even deep brown, like milk chocolate. This slow roasting gives xacuti its dark colour and nutty depth, so don't rush it, but stop before anything blackens.
Blend the roasted spices, coconut and onion with the garlic, ginger and water for 2–3 minutes to a very smooth, thick paste.

Heat the 2 tablespoons of oil in the saucepan over medium heat and fry the chopped onion for 6–8 minutes until golden. Add the xacuti paste and fry for 5–6 minutes, stirring, until it darkens further and oil appears at the edges.

Add the chicken and stir for 5 minutes to coat every piece. Pour in the water, bring to a simmer, cover and cook over low heat for 25 minutes, stirring now and then, until the chicken is tender and reaches 74 °C near the bone.

Stir in the tamarind, nutmeg and salt and simmer uncovered for 2–3 minutes, until the gravy is thick and clings to the chicken. Rest for 10 minutes, then serve with Goan pão (soft bread rolls), chapati or rice.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Lamb xacuti is equally popular in Goa: use 900 g boneless lamb and simmer for 60–70 minutes in step 6.

recipes.name: Laal maas
recipes.description: Rajasthan's fiery red mutton curry, cooked in ghee with a paste of dried red chillies, plenty of garlic and yogurt until the meat is falling-apart tender and the gravy glows deep red.

ingredients.name: Mathania or Kashmiri dried red chillies
Hot water, for soaking the chillies

steps.t: Soak the dried chillies in the hot water for 30 minutes, then blend them with their soaking water to a smooth red paste. Use fewer chillies for a milder curry; Mathania chillies are hot, Kashmiri ones mostly add colour.
Mix the mutton with the yogurt, garlic paste, ground coriander, turmeric and salt. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 1 hour, or overnight.

Heat the ghee in the heavy pot over medium heat. Add the black and green cardamom, cloves, bay leaves and cumin and let them sizzle for 30 seconds. Add the onions and fry, stirring often, for 12–15 minutes until deep golden brown.

Turn the heat up, add the mutton with its marinade and fry, stirring and scraping, for 10–12 minutes, until the yogurt has been absorbed and the meat is browned. This frying (bhunao) is where the flavour builds.
Add the chilli paste and chilli powder and cook, stirring, for 5 minutes, until the ghee rises to the surface and turns brilliant red.

Pour in the hot water, bring to a simmer, cover and cook over low heat for 75–90 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes and adding a splash of water if it sticks. It is ready when the meat comes away from the bone easily and the gravy is thick, with a layer of red ghee on top.
Rest for 10 minutes, scatter with coriander and serve with bajra (millet) roti, chapati or plain rice, and something cooling such as raita.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
safety: Cook mutton (goat) until browned on the outside; slow-cooked pieces are safe once tender and steaming hot throughout.
notes: For the traditional smoky finish (dhungar), put a small bowl in the pot with a red-hot piece of charcoal, pour a teaspoon of ghee over it and cover for 5 minutes.

recipes.name: Rogan josh
recipes.description: Kashmir's celebrated lamb curry: lamb seared in mustard oil and braised with yogurt, Kashmiri chilli, fennel and dry ginger until tender, under a glossy red layer of spiced oil (rogan).

ingredients.name: Lamb shoulder or leg, on the bone

steps.t: Heat the mustard oil in the heavy pot over high heat until it just smokes, then take it off the heat for a minute to cool slightly. Heating mustard oil this far mellows its raw, sharp taste.

Return the pot to medium-high heat and brown the lamb in two batches for 4–5 minutes each, turning, until well coloured on all sides. Return all the lamb to the pot, add the salt and the asafoetida water and stir.

Add the black and green cardamom, cloves, cinnamon and bay leaves and fry for 1 minute. Add the chilli paste and stir for 2 minutes, until the oil turns deep red; the water in the paste stops the chilli from scorching.

Turn the heat to low. Add the yogurt a few spoonfuls at a time, stirring constantly after each addition, so it blends in without splitting. Keep stirring for 5–8 minutes, until the yogurt has been absorbed and the oil begins to separate again.

Stir in the ground fennel and dry ginger, then pour in the hot water. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook over low heat for 60–80 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes, until the lamb is very tender and the gravy has reduced, with a layer of red oil on the surface.
Sprinkle over the garam masala, cover and rest off the heat for 10 minutes. Serve with plain steamed rice, the way it is eaten in Kashmir.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Kashmiri Pandit cooks use no onion, garlic or tomato; Kashmiri Muslim versions add fried shallots and the red flower extract maval for colour.

recipes.name: Dal tadka (yellow dal)
recipes.description: The roadside-dhaba favourite: creamy yellow toor and moong dal cooked with an onion-tomato masala and finished with a smoking-hot double tadka of ghee, garlic and red chillies.

steps.t: Soak the rinsed dals in water for 20 minutes if you have time; it shortens the cooking. Drain and cook them with the turmeric and the 900 ml of water: about 12 minutes in a pressure cooker once it reaches pressure, or 35–40 minutes simmering, half-covered, in a saucepan, skimming the foam at the start.
When the dal is completely soft, whisk it until creamy with a few whole grains left, and stir in the salt. It should pour slowly from a ladle; add hot water to loosen it.

For the masala, heat the 2 tablespoons of ghee in the frying pan over medium heat, add the cumin seeds and let them crackle for a few seconds. Add the onion and fry for 6–7 minutes until golden, then the ginger, garlic and green chillies for 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes, chilli powder and ground coriander and cook for 5–6 minutes, mashing, until the tomatoes have broken down and the ghee separates from the masala.
Tip the masala into the dal, add the garam masala and kasuri methi (crush it between your palms first to release its aroma) and simmer together for 5 minutes, stirring now and then.

For the final tadka, heat the tablespoon of ghee in the small pan over medium-high heat until very hot. Add the sliced garlic and dried chillies and fry for 40–60 seconds until the garlic is light golden. Take the pan off the heat, add the asafoetida and chilli powder (they should sizzle and turn the ghee red, not burn) and pour it all over the dal.
Scatter with coriander and serve straight away, while the tadka still sizzles, with jeera rice, plain rice or roti.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate up to 4 days; dal thickens as it cools.
recipes.reheating: Loosen with hot water and reheat until bubbling.

recipes.name: Khaman dhokla
recipes.description: Gujarat's light, spongy steamed gram-flour cakes, soaked with a sweet-sour tempering of mustard seeds, sesame, green chillies and curry leaves.
equipment: Steamer or large pot with a rack and lid
20 cm round or square cake tin

ingredients.name: Fruit salt (Eno), or 3/4 tsp bicarbonate of soda

steps.t: Bring 5 cm of water to the boil in the steamer and oil the cake tin. Have everything ready before you add the fruit salt, because the batter must go into the steamer the moment it foams.

Whisk the gram flour, semolina, sugar, salt, lemon juice, ginger, green chilli paste, turmeric, oil and water into a smooth, lump-free batter, about as thick as pancake batter. Leave it to rest for 10 minutes so the flour hydrates.

Sprinkle the fruit salt over the batter with a teaspoon of water and whisk briskly in one direction for 10–15 seconds, until the batter turns pale, frothy and roughly doubles. Pour it straight into the tin and tap it once on the counter.

Set the tin in the steamer, cover and steam over medium-high heat for 15–18 minutes, until the dhokla has risen, the top is springy and a skewer pushed into the centre comes out clean. Don't open the lid for the first 12 minutes or it may sink.

Let the dhokla cool for 5 minutes, then run a knife round the edge, turn it out and cut into 4 cm squares. For the tempering, heat the oil in the small pan over medium heat, add the mustard seeds and, when they pop, the sesame seeds, green chillies, curry leaves and asafoetida for a few seconds. Add the water and sugar, boil for 1 minute until the sugar dissolves, then stir in the lemon juice.
Spoon the hot tempering evenly over the dhokla squares so they soak it up and turn moist and spongy. Scatter with coriander and serve warm or at room temperature with green chutney.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate in a covered box within 2 hours; eat within 2 days.
notes: If your dhokla is dense, the batter waited too long after the fruit salt went in, or the steamer wasn't boiling hard.

recipes.name: Punjabi samosa
recipes.description: Tall, blistered samosas with a crisp, flaky ajwain pastry around spiced potato and peas, fried slowly so the crust stays crunchy for hours.

steps.t: For the pastry, mix the flour, ajwain and salt, add the oil and rub it in with your fingertips for 2–3 minutes, until the flour looks like breadcrumbs and holds its shape when you squeeze a handful. This step (moyan) is what makes the crust short and flaky.
Add the cold water a little at a time and knead for 2–3 minutes into a firm, stiff dough; it should be much tighter than chapati dough, or the pastry will be soft. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

For the filling, boil the potatoes in their skins for 20 minutes until tender, then peel and crumble them into small chunks. Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat, add the cumin, crushed coriander and fennel and fry for 30 seconds, then add the ginger, green chillies and peas and cook for 3 minutes. Add the potatoes and all the remaining filling ingredients, toss for 2–3 minutes and spread out on a plate to cool completely.

Divide the dough into 6 balls and roll each into an oval about 20 × 15 cm. Cut each oval in half across the middle. Take a half, wet the straight edge with water, and fold it into a cone, overlapping the wet edge by 1 cm and pressing it firmly to seal.

Fill each cone with about 2 heaped tablespoons of filling, pressing it down gently and leaving 1 cm free at the top. Wet the inside of the open edge, make a small pleat at the back so the samosa stands up, and pinch it shut. Keep the finished samosas under a cloth.

Heat the oil in the kadhai to only 140–150 °C, which is lower than for most frying. Fry the samosas, 4–5 at a time, for 12–15 minutes, turning occasionally. They will rise slowly and the pastry will become pale golden, covered in tiny blisters; frying them hot from the start gives a soft, bubbly crust.
Raise the heat to 170 °C for the last 2 minutes to give them a deeper golden colour, then lift out and drain upright on a rack. Let the oil cool back to 145 °C before the next batch.
Serve warm with tamarind and mint chutneys, or with chana masala as samosa chaat.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate cooled samosas within 2 hours and eat within 3 days; uncooked samosas freeze well.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a 180 °C oven for 10–12 minutes.
notes: Freeze shaped, unfried samosas on a tray, then bag them; fry from frozen at 140 °C for 18–20 minutes.

recipes.name: Mango lassi
recipes.description: A thick, cold blend of ripe mango, yogurt and a little milk with a hint of cardamom: the sweet lassi of Punjab made with the summer's best mangoes.

ingredients.name: Ripe mango flesh (Alphonso, Chaunsa or Kesar), or canned mango pulp

steps.t: Chill the mango, yogurt and milk well beforehand; lassi should be served very cold. Peel the mango and cut the flesh away from the stone.
Blend the mango on its own for 30 seconds until completely smooth, with no fibres left.

Add the yogurt, milk, sugar, cardamom and ice cubes and blend for 30–40 seconds, until frothy and thick enough to coat the glass. Taste and add a little more sugar if your mangoes are tart; add a splash more milk if it is too thick to drink.
Pour into tall glasses and serve straight away, topped with chopped pistachios if you like. Lassi separates if it stands, so blend it just before serving.

recipes.storage: Best drunk fresh; refrigerate and drink within 1 day, re-blending before serving.

recipes.name: Masala chai
recipes.description: Strong black tea boiled with milk, fresh ginger and crushed cardamom, cloves, cinnamon and pepper: the sweet, spiced tea of every Indian street corner.

steps.t: Lightly crush the cardamom, cloves, cinnamon and peppercorns in the mortar, just enough to crack them open. Crush the ginger with the flat of a knife.
Bring the water to the boil in the saucepan with the ginger and crushed spices and boil for 2–3 minutes, until the water is fragrant and pale gold.

Add the tea leaves and boil for 1 minute, until the water turns dark brown. Pour in the milk and sugar and bring back to the boil. When the chai foams up to the rim, lift the pan off the heat until it settles, then return it; do this 2–3 times over 3–4 minutes, until the chai is a rich caramel colour.
Strain into cups and serve piping hot, with biscuits, pakoray or a samosa.

recipes.storage: Best made fresh; refrigerate leftovers and drink within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a pan until steaming.

recipes.name: Rasmalai
recipes.description: Soft, spongy discs of fresh chhena cheese cooked in syrup, then soaked in chilled, saffron and cardamom-scented reduced milk with pistachios: a simplified home version of the Bengali classic.
equipment: Wide pot with a lid for the syrup
Muslin or a clean thin cloth

ingredients.name: Whole milk
ingredients.prep: makes about 200 g chhena; the whey is discarded

ingredients.name: Sugar
ingredients.prep: most of the syrup is left over

steps.t: For the ras, bring the litre of milk to the boil in the heavy saucepan, then simmer over medium-low heat for 25–30 minutes, stirring often and scraping the bottom, until reduced by about a third. Stir in the sugar, saffron, cardamom and most of the nuts and keep it warm.

For the chhena, bring the other litre of milk to the boil in a clean pan. Turn off the heat, wait 1 minute, then add the diluted lemon juice a spoonful at a time, stirring gently, until the milk separates into soft white curds and clear greenish whey. Stop adding lemon as soon as this happens.

Pour into the cloth-lined sieve and rinse the curds under cold running water for 30 seconds to wash off the lemon taste. Gather the cloth, squeeze gently and hang it up for 30–45 minutes, until the chhena is moist and crumbly but no longer dripping.

Tip the chhena onto the plate and knead it with the heel of your hand, smearing and gathering it, for 6–8 minutes, until completely smooth, soft and slightly greasy, with no grains left. Divide into 12 pieces, roll each into a smooth ball and flatten into a 4 cm disc with no cracks at the edges; cracks make them break in the syrup.

Bring the sugar and water to a rolling boil in the wide pot. Slide in the discs, cover and boil hard for 10 minutes, then uncover and boil for 5 minutes more. They will roughly double in size. To check, drop one into a glass of water: if it sinks, it is cooked.

Turn off the heat and leave the discs in the syrup for 10 minutes. Lift each one out, press it very gently between two spoons to squeeze out some of the syrup, and slip it into the warm ras so it soaks up the milk instead.
Cool, then chill for at least 4 hours, or overnight. Serve cold, 2 pieces per bowl with plenty of the ras, scattered with the remaining pistachios and almonds.

notes: The leftover sugar syrup can be used to sweeten tea or lemonade, or to make a second batch.

recipes.name: Aloo paratha
recipes.description: Punjab's favourite breakfast: wholewheat flatbreads stuffed with spiced mashed potato, green chilli and coriander, cooked on a tawa with ghee until golden and crisp-spotted.

steps.t: Mix the atta and salt, add the oil and then the water gradually, kneading for 5–7 minutes into a soft, smooth dough that is slightly softer than for plain roti. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.

Peel the boiled potatoes while still warm and mash them until completely smooth; any lumps will tear the dough when you roll it. Let them cool, then mix in the green chillies, ginger, coriander, ajwain, cumin, amchur, chilli powder, garam masala and salt. Taste: the filling should be well seasoned.

Divide the dough and the filling into 4 equal portions each. Roll a dough ball into a 10 cm round, put a ball of filling in the centre and bring the edges up and over it, pleating as you go, then pinch the top to seal and twist off any excess dough. Flatten gently into a thick disc.

Dust the disc with flour and roll it out gently from the centre outwards to an 18–20 cm round, turning it often. If filling breaks through, patch it with a pinch of flour. Heat the tawa over medium-high heat.
Lay the paratha on the hot tawa and cook for about 1 minute, until small bubbles appear and the underside is dry with light brown spots. Flip and cook the second side for 1 minute.
