Spread a teaspoon of ghee over the top, flip, and press the edges down with the spatula so the paratha puffs and browns evenly, about 1 minute. Spread ghee on the second side, flip again and cook for 1 minute more, until both sides are golden and crisp in spots.
Keep warm wrapped in a clean cloth while you cook the rest. Serve hot with a knob of white butter, plain yogurt and mango or lime pickle.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate cooked parathas within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat on a hot tawa for 1 minute per side.
notes: Gobi (cauliflower) and mooli (radish) parathas use the same method; squeeze the grated vegetable dry first.

recipes.name: Bhuna khichuri
recipes.description: Bangladesh's rainy-day rice: fragrant short-grain rice and roasted moong dal fried in ghee with onions and whole spices, then steamed until each grain stays separate. Classic with beef bhuna or egg curry.
equipment: Heavy pot with a tight lid

ingredients.name: Chinigura or other small-grain aromatic rice (or basmati)

steps.t: Dry-roast the moong dal in the frying pan over medium heat for 4–5 minutes, stirring, until it smells nutty and a few grains turn golden; this keeps the dal whole and gives bhuna khichuri its toasty flavour. Wash the dal and rice together in the sieve until the water runs clear and leave to drain for 15 minutes.

Heat the ghee and oil in the heavy pot over medium heat. Add the bay leaves, cinnamon, cardamom and cloves and let them sizzle for 30 seconds. Add the onions and fry for 8–10 minutes, stirring, until golden brown; lift out a spoonful for garnish.

Add the ginger and garlic pastes, turmeric, chilli powder and cumin with 2 tablespoons of water and fry for 1–2 minutes until the raw smell goes and the oil separates. This frying of the spice paste is what bhuna means.
Add the drained rice and dal and fry, stirring gently but continuously, for 5–6 minutes, until every grain is coated, looks slightly translucent at the edges and smells toasted.

Pour in the hot water, add the salt and green chillies and bring to the boil. Cover tightly and cook over low heat for 15–18 minutes, until the water has been absorbed and the rice and dal are tender but separate.
Turn off the heat and leave covered for 5 minutes, then fluff gently with a fork. Top with the reserved onions and serve hot with beef kala bhuna, egg curry, fried aubergine (begun bhaja) and pickle.

recipes.reheating: Sprinkle with water and reheat, covered, until steaming hot.

recipes.name: Beef kala bhuna
recipes.description: Chittagong's famous 'black' beef: beef braised in mustard oil with onions and a roasted whole-spice masala, then fried for a long time until almost black, dry and intensely spiced.
equipment: Heavy, wide pot or kadhai with a lid

ingredients.name: Beef chuck with a little fat

steps.t: Dry-roast the coriander seeds, cumin, peppercorns, both cardamoms, cloves, cinnamon and dried chillies in the frying pan over medium-low heat for 3–4 minutes, shaking it, until fragrant and a shade darker. Cool and grind to a fine powder with the nutmeg and mace. This is the kala bhuna masala.

Mix the beef with the ginger and garlic pastes, chilli powder, turmeric, ground coriander, ground cumin, salt, 2 tablespoons of the mustard oil and half the kala bhuna masala. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 1 hour, or overnight.

Heat the remaining mustard oil in the heavy pot over high heat until it just smokes, then lower the heat to medium. Add the bay leaves and onions and fry for 10–12 minutes, stirring, until golden brown.
Add the beef and its marinade, turn the heat to high and stir for 8–10 minutes, until the meat is browned and the liquid it releases has mostly evaporated.
Cover and cook over low heat for 70–90 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes and adding a splash of hot water whenever it starts to stick, until the beef is tender when pierced with a knife.

Now the long fry that gives the dish its name. Uncover, add the remaining kala bhuna masala and the green chillies and cook over medium heat for 30–40 minutes, stirring and scraping the bottom every few minutes. The beef darkens from brown to almost black, the gravy disappears and the oil separates and coats the meat. Don't rush it with high heat or the spices burn.
Taste for salt and serve hot with plain rice, bhuna khichuri or paratha. Like most bhunas, it tastes even better the next day.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Mezbani beef, Chittagong's other famous beef dish, uses a similar spice mix but keeps a thin gravy.

recipes.name: Chingri malai curry (prawns in coconut milk)
recipes.description: Large prawns simmered in a mellow, gently sweet coconut milk gravy with onion, ginger, cumin and whole spices: the dish served at Bengali celebrations on both sides of the border.

steps.t: Rub the prawns with half the turmeric and half the salt and leave for 10 minutes.

Heat the mustard oil in the pan over high heat until it just smokes, then lower to medium. Sear the prawns for about 1 minute per side, until they turn pink on the outside but are not cooked through, and lift them out.
Add the bay leaf, cinnamon, cardamom and cloves to the oil and stir for 20 seconds. Add the grated onion and fry for 5 minutes, stirring, until it turns light golden and the raw smell has gone.
Add the ginger paste, chilli powder, cumin and remaining turmeric with 2 tablespoons of water and fry for 2 minutes, until the oil separates from the spices.
Pour in the coconut milk, add the remaining salt, the green chillies and sugar and simmer for 5 minutes, stirring now and then, until the gravy thickens slightly.

Return the prawns and simmer for 3–4 minutes, until they are curled into a loose C shape and opaque all the way through; a tight O shape means they are overcooked. Stir in the ghee and garam masala and take off the heat.
Serve hot with plain steamed rice; the gravy is meant to be generous.

recipes.reheating: Reheat gently until just bubbling; prawns toughen if boiled.
notes: For the full traditional version, cook the prawns with their heads on; the juices in the heads enrich the gravy.

recipes.name: Aloo bhorta (mashed potato with mustard oil)
recipes.description: Bangladesh's simplest comfort food: hot potatoes mashed by hand with raw mustard oil, sliced onion, toasted dried chillies, coriander and salt, eaten with rice and dal.

steps.t: Boil the potatoes in their skins in salted water for 15–20 minutes, until a knife slides into the centre without resistance.

While they cook, toast the dried chillies in the small dry pan over medium heat for 1–2 minutes, turning them, until they darken, puff slightly and smell smoky; don't let them blacken. Crush them with your fingers or a spoon.
Drain and peel the potatoes while they are still hot. Mash them in the bowl with your hand or a fork until smooth with a few small lumps.

Add the onion, crushed chillies, coriander, salt and mustard oil and squeeze and knead everything together with your fingers for a minute, until evenly mixed; the raw mustard oil should make your nose tingle. Taste and add more oil, chilli or salt.
Shape into a mound or small balls and serve warm or at room temperature with plain rice and dal, the way it is eaten for an everyday Bangladeshi lunch.

recipes.name: Mishti doi (sweet set yogurt)
recipes.description: Bengal's famous sweet yogurt: milk reduced and sweetened with caramelised sugar, then set slowly in clay pots into a thick, creamy, gently tangy dessert.
equipment: Small heavy pan for the caramel

ingredients.name: Plain yogurt with live cultures, as a starter

steps.t: Bring the milk to the boil in the heavy saucepan, then simmer over medium-low heat for 20–25 minutes, stirring often and scraping the bottom, until it has reduced to about 700 ml and looks creamy.

Meanwhile, put 60 g of the sugar in the small pan over medium heat. Leave it until it starts to melt at the edges, then swirl the pan until all the sugar has melted into a deep amber caramel, 4–5 minutes. Watch closely: a few seconds too long and it turns bitter.

Take the caramel off the heat and, standing back, pour in a ladleful of the hot milk; it will bubble up and the caramel will harden. Stir over low heat until it dissolves again, then pour it into the rest of the milk with the remaining sugar and stir until smooth and light brown.

Let the milk cool until it feels warm but not hot on your finger, about 40–45 °C. If it is too hot it kills the culture; too cold and it won't set. Whisk the starter yogurt with a few spoonfuls of the milk, then stir it into the pan.

Pour into the clay pots or ramekins, cover with a plate or foil and leave undisturbed in a warm place, such as an oven with only the light on, for 8–10 hours, until set; a spoon should stand up in it. Clay pots absorb some moisture and make the doi extra thick.
Chill for at least 2 hours, then serve cold, straight from the pots.

notes: In winter, Bengalis make it with date-palm jaggery (nolen gur) instead of caramelised sugar.

recipes.name: Chicken kottu roti
recipes.description: Sri Lanka's best-loved street food: flaky godamba roti chopped and tossed on a hot griddle with chicken curry, egg, leeks, carrot and cabbage to the clatter of two metal blades.
equipment: Large flat griddle or very large wok
Two metal spatulas or bench scrapers

steps.t: Make the roti dough at least 2 hours ahead. Mix the flour, salt and sugar, add the water gradually and knead for 8–10 minutes into a very soft, smooth, elastic dough. Divide into 6 balls, roll each in a tablespoon of the oil to coat, cover and rest for at least 2 hours, or overnight in the fridge. Resting is what lets the dough stretch paper-thin.

For the curry, heat the oil in the saucepan over medium heat and fry the cinnamon, onion, garlic, ginger and curry leaves for 5 minutes until soft. Add the chicken, curry powder, chilli powder and turmeric and stir for 3 minutes, then add the tomato, water and salt. Simmer, covered, for 20 minutes until the chicken is tender and cooked through (74 °C). Shred the chicken roughly, keeping the gravy.

Oil the work surface. Flatten a dough ball with your palm, then stretch it outwards with oiled fingers, lifting and pulling the edges, until it is very thin and almost see-through, about 40 cm across. Fold the edges in to make a square of about 20 cm.

Cook each roti on the hot, dry griddle over medium-high heat for 1–2 minutes per side, until cooked through with light golden patches. Stack them, cool for a few minutes, then roll up and slice into strips about 1 cm wide.

Heat the oil for the kottu on the griddle over high heat. Fry the onion, leek, carrot, cabbage, green chillies and curry leaves for 3–4 minutes, until wilted but still crunchy. Push them aside, crack the eggs onto the empty space and scramble until just set.

Add the roti strips, shredded chicken and a few ladles of the curry gravy. Chop and toss everything together with the two spatulas for 4–5 minutes, until the roti has soaked up the gravy and broken into small pieces, with some edges crisp. Season with black pepper and salt.
Serve straight away, piled high, with the remaining curry gravy in a bowl on the side for spooning over.

recipes.reheating: Reheat in a hot pan, tossing, until steaming hot throughout.
notes: Short of time? Use 6 frozen flaky parathas, cooked and cut into strips, instead of homemade godamba roti.

recipes.name: Parippu (Sri Lankan dhal curry)
recipes.description: The creamy, golden lentil curry on every Sri Lankan rice-and-curry plate: red lentils simmered with turmeric and coconut milk, finished with a tempering of mustard seeds, shallots and dried chillies.

steps.t: Put the lentils, water, turmeric, onion, green chillies, garlic and half the curry leaves in the saucepan and bring to the boil over high heat. Skim off the foam, then simmer, half-covered, for 12–15 minutes, stirring now and then, until the lentils are soft and starting to break down.
Stir in the coconut milk and salt and simmer gently for 5 minutes, until creamy. The parippu should be thick but pourable; add a splash of water if it gets too thick.

For the tempering, heat the coconut oil in the small pan over medium heat. Add the mustard seeds and, when they pop, the dried chillies, shallots and remaining curry leaves. Fry for 2–3 minutes, stirring, until the shallots are golden brown.
Pour the tempering over the parippu and stir it through. Serve hot with rice, pol sambol and a meat or fish curry, or with roti or bread for breakfast.

recipes.reheating: Loosen with a splash of water and reheat until bubbling.
notes: A strip of pandan (rampe) leaf and a small piece of cinnamon in step 1 give the authentic Sri Lankan aroma.

recipes.name: Pol sambol (coconut relish)
recipes.description: Freshly grated coconut pounded with red chilli, shallots, salt and lime until rosy red: the fiery, tangy relish that comes with hoppers, string hoppers, rice and bread in every Sri Lankan home.
equipment: Mortar and pestle (or a small food processor)

ingredients.name: Sri Lankan chilli powder or chilli flakes

steps.t: Pound the shallots, chilli powder and salt (and the Maldive fish, if using) in the mortar for 1–2 minutes into a rough, wet red paste. The salt helps break down the shallots.

Add the coconut a handful at a time and keep pounding and mixing for 2–3 minutes, until the coconut turns evenly orange-red and slightly moist. In a food processor, pulse in short bursts so the coconut stays fluffy rather than turning into a paste.
Tip into the bowl, squeeze over the lime juice and mix with your fingertips. Taste: it should be hot, salty and sharp in equal measure, so adjust the chilli, salt and lime.
Serve straight away with hoppers, string hoppers, kiri bath, rice and curry, or simply spread on buttered bread.

recipes.storage: Best eaten the day it is made; refrigerate and eat within 1 day.
notes: Freshly grated coconut is essential; desiccated coconut soaked in hot water for 15 minutes is a passable substitute.

recipes.name: Sri Lankan chicken curry
recipes.description: A dark, aromatic chicken curry made with freshly roasted curry powder, curry leaves, lemongrass and cinnamon, finished with coconut milk: the centrepiece of a Sunday rice-and-curry lunch.
equipment: Heavy frying pan for roasting spices

steps.t: Make the roasted curry powder: dry-roast all its ingredients in the frying pan over medium-low heat for 5–7 minutes, stirring constantly, until they are a deep, even brown like coffee beans and smell intensely toasty, but not burnt. Cool and grind to a fine powder.
Mix the chicken with 2 tablespoons of the roasted curry powder, the chilli powder, turmeric, vinegar and salt. Leave to marinate for 30 minutes, or up to 12 hours in the fridge.
Heat the coconut oil in the heavy pot over medium heat. Add the cinnamon, onions, curry leaves and lemongrass and fry for 6–8 minutes, stirring, until the onions are golden.
Add the garlic, ginger and green chillies and stir for 2 minutes, then add the chicken and fry, turning, for 5–6 minutes until it is coated and lightly browned.
Add the tomato and water, bring to a simmer, cover and cook over low heat for 25 minutes, stirring now and then, until the chicken is tender and reaches 74 °C near the bone.
Stir in the coconut milk and the rest of the curry powder and simmer uncovered for 8–10 minutes, until the gravy is thick, dark and glossy. Remove the lemongrass and cinnamon.
Rest for 10 minutes and serve with rice, parippu, pol sambol and a vegetable curry for a full rice-and-curry meal.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Add a 5 cm piece of pandan (rampe) leaf with the curry leaves if you can find it.

recipes.name: Watalappan (jaggery coconut custard)
recipes.description: A steamed custard of coconut milk, eggs and dark kithul jaggery spiced with cardamom and nutmeg, with a honeycomb texture and cashews on top; the Eid dessert of Sri Lanka's Muslim community.
equipment: Steamer or deep roasting tin for a water bath

steps.t: Melt the jaggery with the water in the small saucepan over low heat, stirring, for 3–4 minutes until completely dissolved. Strain it to remove any grit and let it cool until just warm.
Whisk the eggs gently in a large bowl until well mixed but not frothy; too much air gives bubbles on top. Stir in the coconut milk, then the jaggery syrup, cardamom, nutmeg, cloves and salt.
Strain the mixture through a sieve into the greased bowl or ramekins and skim off any foam with a spoon. Cover tightly with foil.

Steam over gently simmering water for 40–50 minutes (25–30 minutes for ramekins), or bake in a water bath at 160 °C for 50–60 minutes, until set at the edges with a slight wobble in the centre and a knife inserted near the middle comes out clean. Keep the heat gentle so the custard doesn't curdle.
Scatter the toasted cashews over the top. Let it cool, then chill for at least 3 hours, until firm. A good watalappan has a slightly porous, honeycomb texture when cut.
Serve cold, in spoonfuls, after the Eid meal or at any celebration.

recipes.name: Kiri bath (coconut milk rice)
recipes.description: Rice cooked soft and creamy in coconut milk, pressed flat and cut into diamonds: Sri Lanka's auspicious breakfast for New Year and the first day of each month, served with a fiery onion sambol.
equipment: Medium heavy saucepan with a lid

ingredients.name: Short-grain white rice (such as samba or raw rice)

steps.t: Rinse the rice in two or three changes of cold water, swirling it with your hand, until the water is only slightly cloudy. Leaving a little surface starch is what makes kiri bath creamy enough to set into a slab.
Put the rice and water in the saucepan, bring to the boil, then cover and simmer over low heat for 15 minutes, until the rice is very soft and most of the water has been absorbed.

Stir in the coconut milk and salt and cook, uncovered, over low heat for 8–10 minutes, stirring often, until the rice has absorbed the coconut milk and looks thick, sticky and creamy. It should hold together in a mass.

Tip the rice onto the plate and spread it into an even slab about 2–3 cm thick, smoothing the top with a spatula or a piece of banana leaf dipped in water. Leave for 10 minutes to firm up, then cut into diamonds.
For the lunu miris, pound the shallots, chilli flakes and salt (and Maldive fish, if using) in the mortar to a coarse red paste, then mix in the lime juice.
Serve the kiri bath warm with lunu miris, or the sweet way with jaggery and ripe bananas.

recipes.storage: Best eaten the day it is made; refrigerate within 2 hours.
recipes.reheating: Steam or microwave, covered, until steaming hot.

recipes.name: Chicken momo with tomato achar
recipes.description: Kathmandu's beloved steamed dumplings: thin wrappers pleated around a juicy chicken filling with onion, coriander, ginger and timur, served with a smoky roasted tomato and sesame achar.
equipment: Steamer (bamboo or metal) with a lid

steps.t: Mix the flour and salt, add the oil and then the water gradually, kneading for 5–7 minutes into a firm, smooth dough that doesn't stick to your hands. Cover and rest for 30 minutes so it rolls out thin without springing back.

Put all the filling ingredients in a bowl and mix vigorously with your hand in one direction for 2–3 minutes, until the mince turns sticky and paste-like. This, with the butter and water, keeps the filling juicy and in one piece. Chill while you make the achar.

For the achar, roast the tomatoes in the dry frying pan over medium-high heat (or directly over a gas flame) for 8–10 minutes, turning, until the skins are blistered and charred in places; toast the dried chillies and garlic alongside for 1–2 minutes. Toast the sesame seeds separately for 2 minutes until golden. Blend everything with the timur, coriander, lemon juice and salt to a coarse sauce.
Heat the mustard oil in a small pan until it smokes, add the fenugreek seeds and let them turn dark brown, about 20 seconds, then pour the oil over the achar and stir. Set aside.

Roll the dough into a long rope and cut it into 40 pieces of about 11 g each. Roll each into a circle about 8 cm across, rolling the edges thinner than the centre; keep the rest covered so it doesn't dry out.

To fold, hold a wrapper in one palm, put a heaped teaspoon of filling in the centre and use your other thumb and forefinger to make small overlapping pleats round the edge, turning the wrapper as you go, until the pleats meet at the top. Pinch and twist the top to seal into a round purse. Half-moons with pleats along one side are fine too.

Brush the steamer with oil and arrange the momos 2 cm apart. Steam over rapidly boiling water, covered, for 10–12 minutes, until the wrappers look translucent and slightly shiny and the filling is firm; a momo cut open should show no pink, with clear juices (74 °C). Steam in batches.
Serve the momos hot from the steamer with the tomato achar for dipping.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 2 days; uncooked momos freeze well on a tray.
recipes.reheating: Re-steam for 4–5 minutes until steaming hot throughout.
notes: Freeze uncooked momos on a floured tray, then bag them; steam from frozen for 15 minutes.
Water buffalo ('buff') is the classic Kathmandu filling; lean beef mince is the nearest substitute.

recipes.name: Jhol momo
recipes.description: Steamed chicken momos served swimming in jhol: a warm, tangy soup of roasted tomato, sesame, timur and chilli. A Kathmandu favourite on cold evenings.
equipment: Steamer (bamboo or metal) with a lid

steps.t: Knead the flour, salt, oil and water for 5–7 minutes into a firm, smooth dough, cover and rest for 30 minutes. Meanwhile, beat all the filling ingredients together with your hand in one direction for 2–3 minutes until sticky, then chill.

For the jhol, char the tomatoes in a dry frying pan over medium-high heat for 8–10 minutes, turning, until blistered and soft. In the same pan, toast the sesame seeds for 2 minutes until golden and the dried chillies for 1 minute, taking care that neither burns.

Blend the tomatoes, sesame, chillies, garlic, ginger, timur, cumin, turmeric and coriander with half the stock until very smooth. Pour into the saucepan with the rest of the stock and the salt and simmer for 10 minutes. It should be the thickness of a light soup.

Heat the mustard oil in a small pan until it smokes, add the fenugreek seeds for 20 seconds until dark brown, then pour into the jhol. Stir in the lemon juice, taste for salt and sourness and keep it hot over the lowest heat.

Cut the dough into 40 pieces and roll each into an 8 cm circle, thinner at the edges. Put a teaspoon of filling in the centre of each, fold the wrapper in half into a half-moon and pinch the edge into a row of small pleats to seal it.

Arrange the momos in the oiled steamer, 2 cm apart, and steam over rapidly boiling water for 10–12 minutes, until the wrappers turn translucent and a momo cut open shows no pink and clear juices (74 °C). Steam in batches.
Put 10 hot momos in each wide bowl and ladle over plenty of steaming jhol so they are half submerged. Scatter with a little extra coriander and serve straight away, before the wrappers soften.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate momos and jhol separately within 2 hours; eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Re-steam the momos and reheat the jhol separately until steaming hot.
notes: Many Kathmandu cooks add a handful of roasted soybeans (bhatmas) or peanuts to the jhol for extra body.

recipes.name: Dal bhat tarkari
recipes.description: Nepal's twice-daily meal: steamed rice (bhat), a thin lentil soup tempered with ghee, garlic and jimbu (dal), and a turmeric-gold potato and cauliflower curry (tarkari), with pickle on the side.
equipment: Saucepan with a lid for the rice
Kadhai or deep frying pan with a lid

steps.t: Soak the rinsed rice in fresh water for 15 minutes, then drain. Bring the rice and 550 ml water to the boil in the saucepan, cover, turn the heat to the lowest setting and cook for 15 minutes. Turn off the heat and leave covered for 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork.

For the dal, bring the lentils, water, turmeric and ginger to the boil, skim off the foam and simmer, half-covered, for 20 minutes, until the lentils have dissolved. Whisk well and add the salt; Nepali dal is thinner than Indian dal, like a soup you can pour over rice.

Heat the ghee in the small pan over medium heat, add the cumin, garlic and jimbu (if using) and fry for about 1 minute, until the garlic is light gold and the jimbu smells oniony. Pour it into the dal, cover and keep warm.

For the tarkari, heat the mustard oil in the kadhai over high heat until it just smokes, then lower to medium. Add the fenugreek seeds and let them turn dark brown, about 20 seconds, then add the cumin seeds.

Add the potatoes and fry for 5 minutes, stirring, until the edges turn golden. Add the cauliflower, garlic, ginger, green chillies, turmeric, chilli powder, ground coriander and salt and toss until everything is yellow.

Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 12–15 minutes, stirring every few minutes and adding a splash of water if it sticks, until the potatoes and cauliflower are tender. Add the tomato and cook uncovered for 3 minutes until soft, then stir in the coriander.

Serve the way it is eaten across Nepal: a mound of rice in the centre of the plate, a bowl of dal to pour over it a little at a time, the tarkari alongside and a spoonful of pickle (achar) and some sautéed greens if you have them.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Jimbu is a dried Himalayan allium sold in Nepali shops; a pinch of asafoetida or extra garlic is the usual substitute.

recipes.name: Kwati (sprouted bean soup)
recipes.description: A thick, warming Newari soup of nine kinds of sprouted beans cooked with ajwain, garlic, ginger and tomato, made for the festival of Janai Purnima and on cold monsoon days.
equipment: Large heavy pot or pressure cooker
Large bowls for soaking and sprouting

steps.t: Start 3–4 days ahead. Rinse the beans, cover with plenty of warm water and soak for 12 hours. Drain, cover the bowl with a damp cloth and leave in a warm, dark place, rinsing and draining twice a day, for 2–3 days, until most beans have sprouted tails of 0.5–1 cm. Some, like kidney beans, sprout less; that's fine.

Rinse the sprouted beans well. Heat the mustard oil in the pot over high heat until it just smokes, then lower to medium and add the ajwain, fenugreek, bay leaves and dried chillies. Let them sizzle for 20–30 seconds, until the fenugreek turns dark brown.

Add the onion and fry for 5–6 minutes until golden, then the garlic and ginger for 1 minute. Add the tomatoes, turmeric, cumin, coriander, chilli powder and salt and cook for 4–5 minutes until the tomatoes soften.

Add the sprouted beans and stir-fry for 5 minutes, so they absorb the spices. Pour in the water and bring to a rolling boil; boil hard for at least 10 minutes, which is essential to make kidney beans safe.

Lower the heat, cover and simmer for 45–60 minutes (or pressure-cook for 20–25 minutes), until every kind of bean is completely tender, including the largest kidney beans. Mash a ladleful against the side of the pot to thicken the soup slightly.
Stir in the timur and garam masala, taste for salt and simmer for 2 minutes more. Serve hot, scattered with coriander, as a soup on its own or with rice or beaten rice (chiura).

recipes.reheating: Reheat until boiling, adding water if it has thickened.
safety: Boil the beans hard for at least 10 minutes before simmering; undercooked kidney beans can cause food poisoning.
notes: Bean weights are dry weights; any mix of 7–9 kinds works, including soybeans and field peas.

recipes.name: Sel roti
recipes.description: Nepal's festive ring-shaped bread: a sweet batter of soaked ground rice, banana and ghee poured into hot oil in a circle and fried until crisp outside and chewy within.

steps.t: Soak the rice in plenty of water for 8 hours or overnight. Drain it in a sieve and leave it for 30 minutes so it is no longer dripping.

Blend the rice with the sugar, banana, ghee and cardamom, adding the milk a little at a time, for 4–5 minutes, until you have a thick batter that still feels very slightly grainy, like fine semolina, and falls from a spoon in a thick ribbon. Too thin and the rings spread; too thick and they won't flow.
Cover and rest the batter for 1–2 hours at room temperature; it thickens a little and the rings hold their shape better. Stir it well before frying.

Heat the oil in the kadhai to 175 °C. Fill a squeeze bottle with batter, or use your hand: scoop some batter into your palm and let it pour from the side of your fist as you move your hand in a steady circle about 10–12 cm across, so the ring joins up where it started.

The ring sinks briefly, then floats. After about 1 minute, push it under gently with the skewer and flip it once the underside is reddish golden. Fry the second side for 1 minute more, until both sides are deep golden brown.

Lift the sel roti out by threading the skewer through the ring and let it drain upright over the pan, then on a rack. Fry one or two at a time, letting the oil return to 175 °C in between. Don't worry if your first few are uneven; the shape comes with practice.
Serve warm or at room temperature with aloo tarkari or aloo ko achar, yogurt and tea. Sel roti keep well for several days, which is why families make large batches for Tihar.

recipes.storage: Keep in an airtight tin at room temperature for up to 4 days.
notes: If you can't soak and grind rice, use 400 g rice flour mixed with the other ingredients and enough milk to make the same thick batter.

recipes.name: Aloo ko achar (potato sesame salad)
recipes.description: A tangy Nepali potato salad dressed with toasted ground sesame, chilli and lemon, then finished with a sizzling mustard oil, fenugreek and timur tempering.

ingredients.name: Waxy potatoes (about 4 small)
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.t: Boil the potato cubes in salted water for 10–12 minutes, until tender but still holding their shape. Drain and spread out to cool slightly.
Toast the sesame seeds in the dry pan over medium heat for 2–3 minutes, stirring, until golden and starting to pop. Cool for a minute, then grind to a fine powder.
Put the potatoes, cucumber, green chillies, chilli powder, ground sesame, lemon juice, salt and most of the coriander in the bowl and mix gently so every cube is coated.

Heat the mustard oil in the small pan until it just smokes, add the fenugreek seeds and fry for 20 seconds until dark brown, then take off the heat and stir in the turmeric and timur. Pour the sizzling oil over the potatoes and toss.

Leave for 10 minutes for the flavours to soak in, then taste for salt and lemon. Serve at room temperature with the rest of the coriander, alongside sel roti, beaten rice or as part of a snack platter.

recipes.name: Mas huni with roshi
recipes.description: The Maldivian breakfast: tuna rubbed with freshly grated coconut, onion, chilli and lime, scooped up with warm, thin roshi flatbreads and a cup of sweet black tea.

ingredients.name: Tuna in water or brine, drained (or smoked tuna)
Hot green chilli or Scotch bonnet (githeyo mirus)

steps.t: Mix the flour and salt, add the oil and the warm water gradually and knead for 5 minutes into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 15 minutes.

For the mas huni, put the onion, chilli, curry leaves, salt and lime juice in the bowl and squeeze them together hard with your fingertips for about 1 minute. Crushing the onion this way softens it and releases its juice into the lime.

Add the drained tuna, flaked, and the coconut, and keep rubbing and squeezing everything between your fingers for 1–2 minutes, until the tuna and coconut are evenly mixed, moist and fluffy. Taste and add more lime, chilli or salt; it should be sharp and hot.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and roll each very thin, about 18 cm across, dusting with flour. Heat the tawa over medium-high heat.

Cook each roshi for 30–60 seconds per side, until it bubbles and has light brown spots; press the edges with a folded cloth to help it puff. Stack them in a clean tea towel to keep soft and warm while you cook the rest.
Serve the mas huni in a bowl with the warm roshi. Tear off a piece of roshi and use it to pinch up the mas huni, with sweet black tea and, traditionally, a few slices of papaya or banana on the side.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate mas huni within 2 hours and eat within 1 day; roshi keep 2 days wrapped.
recipes.reheating: Warm roshi on a hot dry pan for a few seconds per side.
notes: In the Maldives it is made with smoked tuna (valhoa mas) or fresh boiled tuna; good canned tuna is what most homes now use.

recipes.name: Garudhiya (tuna broth)
recipes.description: The national dish of the Maldives: a clear, golden broth of fresh tuna simmered with nothing but water and salt, eaten with rice, lime, chilli and raw onion.

ingredients.name: Fresh skipjack or yellowfin tuna, on the bone

steps.t: Rinse the tuna pieces well under cold water to remove any blood, which would cloud the broth. Bones and the head add extra flavour if you have them.

Put the tuna, water and salt in the large pot and bring slowly to the boil over medium heat. As it heats, a grey foam rises; skim it off carefully and continuously for the first 10 minutes. This patient skimming is the secret to a clear garudhiya.

When no more foam appears, lower the heat and simmer gently, uncovered, for 30–35 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily and the broth tastes rich and is a pale golden colour. Don't let it boil hard, or the broth turns cloudy.

While the broth simmers, prepare the accompaniments: slice the onion very thinly, chop the chillies, cut the limes into wedges and cook the rice, if serving. They are what season each bowl, so be generous.
Add the curry leaves for the last 5 minutes, then taste and adjust the salt. Lift out any bones if you like.

Serve the broth and fish pieces in bowls, with rice, lime wedges, sliced onion and chopped chillies on the table. Maldivians mix rice into the broth by hand, adding lime, chilli and onion to taste with every mouthful.

recipes.reheating: Reheat gently until steaming hot.
notes: Leftover broth is traditionally cooked down for hours into rihaakuru, a thick, savoury tuna paste kept as a seasoning.

recipes.name: Mas riha (tuna curry)
recipes.description: Maldivian tuna curry: chunks of fresh tuna simmered in coconut milk with curry leaves, cinnamon, cardamom, fennel and chilli, finished with lime. Eaten with rice or roshi.

ingredients.name: Hot green chilli or Scotch bonnet

steps.t: Toss the tuna cubes with half the chilli powder, half the turmeric and half the salt and leave for 10 minutes. Shake the can of coconut milk, pour half into a jug with the water (thin coconut milk) and keep the rest thick.

Heat the coconut oil in the saucepan over medium heat. Add the curry leaves, cinnamon and cardamom and let them sizzle for 30 seconds. Add the onion, garlic, ginger and chilli and fry for 5–6 minutes, until the onion is soft and golden.
Add the cumin, fennel, coriander, black pepper and the rest of the chilli powder and turmeric with 2 tablespoons of water and stir for 1 minute, until the oil separates and the spices smell toasted.
Pour in the thin coconut milk and the remaining salt, bring to a simmer and cook for 5 minutes so the gravy comes together.
Add the tuna and simmer gently, covered, for 8–10 minutes, shaking the pan now and then rather than stirring, until the fish is opaque and firm all the way through.
Stir in the thick coconut milk and heat for 2 minutes without boiling, then add the lime juice and take off the heat. Serve with plain rice or roshi and a squeeze more lime.

recipes.reheating: Reheat gently until just bubbling.
notes: Skipjack tuna is the everyday Maldivian fish; firm fish such as kingfish or mackerel also work.
